questions.question: The statement $p \to  (q \to  p)$ is equivalent to
questions.key_idea: Rewrite $p\to  q$ as ${\sim}p \vee  q$; then $p \to  (q \to  p)$ collapses to a tautology.
solution: Write the implication as an OR: $p \to  (q \to  p) \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  (q \to  p)$.
Again: $\equiv  {\sim}p \vee  ({\sim}q \vee  p)$.
Regroup: $\equiv  ({\sim}p \vee  p) \vee  {\sim}q$.
${\sim}p \vee  p$ is always true, so the whole statement is a tautology $\mathrm{t}$.
Option (A): $p \to  (p \vee  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  p \vee  q$, and ${\sim}p \vee  p$ is true, so it is also a tautology $\mathrm{t}$.
Two tautologies are always equivalent, so the given statement is equivalent to $p \to  (p \vee  q)$.
Check of the rest: (B), (C), (D) all reduce to $p \to  q$, which is false for $p=T,\ q=F$, so they are not tautologies.
Answer: (A).
questions.correction_note: PDF's third line replaces (~p v p) v ~q by ~p v p v q; that is not an equivalence step (both sides just happen to be tautologies). Rewritten so the step is justified, and options B-D are explicitly rejected.

alternate_solutions.idea: A conditional is false in exactly one way, so look only for the assignment that makes it false.
solution: $p \to  X$ is false only when $p$ is true and $X$ is false.
For $X=q \to  p$: if $p$ is true then $q \to  p$ is true, so $X$ cannot be false. Hence $p \to  (q \to  p)$ is never false: a tautology.
For (A), $X = p \vee  q$: if $p$ is true then $p \vee  q$ is true, so it is also never false: a tautology.
For (B), (C), (D) take $p=T,\ q=F$: then $p \wedge  q$, $p \leftrightarrow  q$ and $p \to  q$ are all false, so each conditional is false.
Only (A) is equivalent to the given tautology.

useful_results: $p \to  (q \to  p)$ is a tautology (a standard axiom: a true statement is implied by anything).
$p \to  (p \wedge  q) \equiv  p \to  q$, $p \to  (p \leftrightarrow  q) \equiv  p \to  q$ and $p \to  (p \to  q) \equiv  p \to  q$: the leading $p$ is absorbed.
A conditional $X \to  Y$ is a tautology iff no assignment makes $X$ true and $Y$ false.
$p \to  (p \vee  q)$ is the 'addition' rule of inference.

questions.question:
Let $p$ be the statement '$x$ is an irrational number', $q$ the statement '$y$ is a transcendental number', and $r$ the statement '$x$ is an irrational number iff $y$ is a transcendental number'.
Statement-1: $r$ is equivalent to either $q$ or $p$.
Statement-2: $r$ is equivalent to ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$.
options: Statement-1 is true, Statement-2 is true; Statement-2 is a correct explanation for Statement-1
Statement-1 is true, Statement-2 is true; Statement-2 is not a correct explanation for Statement-1
Statement-1 is true, Statement-2 is false
Statement-1 is false, Statement-2 is true
questions.key_idea: $r$ is $p \leftrightarrow  q$; compare its truth table with $q \vee  p$ and with ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$.
solution: Here $r : p \leftrightarrow  q$ (x irrational iff y transcendental).
Statement-1 claims $r \equiv  q \vee  p$; Statement-2 claims $r \equiv  {\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$.
Truth table in the order $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF: $p \leftrightarrow  q$ = T, F, F, T.
$q \vee  p$ = T, T, T, F. ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$ = T, F, F, T.
$p \leftrightarrow  q$ differs from $q \vee  p$ in row TF (F against T): Statement-1 is false.
$p \leftrightarrow  q$ equals ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$ in all four rows: Statement-2 is true.
Answer: (D).
questions.correction_note: PDF begins 'Given r : ~p <-> q'. The statement r is 'x irrational iff y transcendental', i.e. p <-> q (the PDF's own table uses p <-> q). Corrected.

alternate_solutions.idea: Negating one side of a biconditional flips it, so ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$ simplifies at once; one counter-example kills Statement-1.
solution: $p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q$ means '$p$ and $q$ differ', which is ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  q)$.
So ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q) \equiv  {\sim}{\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  q) \equiv  p \leftrightarrow  q = r$: Statement-2 is true.
For Statement-1 take $p=T,\ q=F$: then $r = p \leftrightarrow  q$ is false, but $q \vee  p$ is true.
So $r$ is not equivalent to $q \vee  p$: Statement-1 is false. (Same verdict if 'either...or' is read as exclusive or: that is ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  q)$, the opposite of $r$.)
Answer: (D).

useful_results: ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  q) \equiv  p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q \equiv  {\sim}p \leftrightarrow  q$ (negate either one side), and ${\sim}p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q \equiv  p \leftrightarrow  q$.
$p \leftrightarrow  q \equiv  (p \to  q) \wedge  (q \to  p) \equiv  (p \wedge  q) \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q)$.
$p \leftrightarrow  q$ is true exactly when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth value; $p \vee  q$ is true also when they differ, so $p \leftrightarrow  q \not\equiv  p \vee  q$.
Never trust a statement of the form 'either ... or' without deciding whether it is inclusive or exclusive.

questions.question:
Statement-1: ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$ is equivalent to $p \leftrightarrow  q$.
Statement-2: ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$ is a tautology.
options: Statement-1 is true, Statement-2 is true; Statement-2 is not a correct explanation for Statement-1
Statement-1 is true, Statement-2 is false
Statement-1 is false, Statement-2 is true
Statement-1 is true, Statement-2 is true; Statement-2 is a correct explanation for Statement-1
questions.key_idea: Build one truth table with columns $p\leftrightarrow  q$, ${\sim}q$, $p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q$ and ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$.
solution: Compute in the order $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF.
$p \leftrightarrow  q$ = T, F, F, T.
${\sim}q$ = F, T, F, T.
$p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q$ = F, T, T, F.
${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$ = T, F, F, T.
This column is identical to $p \leftrightarrow  q$: Statement-1 is true.
The column is not all T (rows TF and FT are F), so it is not a tautology: Statement-2 is false.
Answer: (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Read the biconditional as 'same truth value'; $p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q$ then says 'different values', whose negation is 'same values'.
solution: $p \leftrightarrow  q$ is true exactly when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth value.
$p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q$ is true exactly when $p$ and ${\sim}q$ agree, i.e. when $p$ and $q$ disagree.
Its negation is true exactly when $p$ and $q$ agree: that is $p \leftrightarrow  q$. Statement-1 is true.
A tautology must be true for every assignment, but with $p=T,\ q=F$ the values disagree, so ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$ is false. Statement-2 is false.
Answer: (B).

useful_results: ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q) \equiv  p \leftrightarrow  q$: negating one side of $\leftrightarrow$ toggles it, and doing it twice cancels.
A statement equivalent to a non-tautology such as $p \leftrightarrow  q$ can never be a tautology.
In 'Statement-1 / Statement-2' items, check each statement on its own first; the 'correct explanation' option only matters when both are true.

questions.question: Let $S$ be a non-empty subset of $\mathbb{R}$. Consider the statement $P$: There is a rational number $x \in S$ such that $x>0$. Which of the following statements is the negation of the statement $P$?
options: There is a rational number $x \in S$ such that $x \le 0$
There is no rational number $x \in S$ such that $x \le 0$
$x \in S$ and $x \le 0 \Rightarrow x$ is not a rational number
questions.key_idea: The negation of 'there exists' is 'for every', and the condition $x>0$ is negated to $x \le 0$.
solution: $P$: there exists a rational $x\in S$ with $x>0$.
${\sim}P$: it is false that such an $x$ exists, i.e. every rational number $x \in S$ satisfies $x \le 0$.
(A) still asserts existence, so it is not the negation.
(B) says no rational $x\in S$ is $\le 0$; this has nothing to do with the positive ones (take $S=\{1\}$: $P$ is true yet (B) is true).
(D) says every non-positive element of $S$ is irrational; for $S=\{1\}$ it is vacuously true although $P$ is true.
Answer: (C).
questions.source_note: PDF gives only the negation line; the rejection of A, B, D was added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the four options on small sets $S$: the negation must be false whenever $P$ is true and true whenever $P$ is false.
solution: Take $S=\{1\}$: $P$ is true, so its negation must be false.
For $S=\{1\}$: (B) is true (no rational $x\in S$ with $x\le0$) and (D) is true (vacuous). So (B), (D) are out.
Take $S=\{-1,1\}$: $P$ is true, so the negation must be false. Here (A) is true ($x=-1$), so (A) is out.
(C) is false for both sets (because $1>0$) and true for $S=\{-1\}$, where $P$ is false: consistent.
Answer: (C).

useful_results: ${\sim}(\exists x\ P(x)) \equiv  \forall x\ {\sim}P(x)$ and ${\sim}(\forall x\ P(x)) \equiv  \exists x\ {\sim}P(x)$.
The negation of $x>0$ is $x \le 0$ (not $x<0$).
A restricted quantifier $\exists x \in S$ becomes $\forall x \in S$ in the negation; the restriction stays.
A counter-example set (like $S=\{1\}$ or $\{-1,1\}$) quickly kills wrong options.

questions.question: Consider the statements $P$: Suman is brilliant; $Q$: Suman is rich; $R$: Suman is honest. The negation of the statement 'Suman is brilliant and dishonest if and only if Suman is rich' can be expressed as
questions.key_idea: Translate first: $(P \wedge  {\sim}R) \leftrightarrow  Q$; negating one side of a biconditional negates the whole biconditional.
solution: 'Brilliant and dishonest' is $P \wedge  {\sim}R$, so the statement is $(P \wedge  {\sim}R) \leftrightarrow  Q$.
Its negation is ${\sim}[(P \wedge  {\sim}R) \leftrightarrow  Q]$.
Negating a biconditional: ${\sim}(X \leftrightarrow  Y) \equiv  ({\sim}X) \leftrightarrow  Y$.
With $X=P \wedge  {\sim}R$, $Y=Q$ this gives ${\sim}(P \wedge  {\sim}R) \leftrightarrow  Q$, which is option (B).
Check the others: for $P=T,R=F,Q=T$ the statement is true so its negation is false, but (A) is true and (D) is true.
For $P=F,R=T,Q=T$ the negation is true, but (C) is false.
Answer: (B).
questions.correction_note: PDF writes the statement as 'brilliant and honest iff rich' and the negation as ~[(P ^ ~R) <-> Q], which mixes honest/dishonest. The statement is (P ^ ~R) <-> Q; the answer B is unaffected. Written out the steps that show B equals the negation.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test assignments: pick truth values where the original statement has a known value and see which options match the negation.
solution: Take $P=T,\ R=F,\ Q=T$: the statement $(P \wedge  {\sim}R) \leftrightarrow  Q$ is $T \leftrightarrow  T=T$, so its negation is F.

Evaluate options: (A) ${\sim}Q \leftrightarrow  ({\sim}P \wedge  R)$ = $F \leftrightarrow  F$ = T; (B) ${\sim}(P \wedge  {\sim}R) \leftrightarrow  Q$ = $F \leftrightarrow  T$ = F; (C) ${\sim}P \wedge (\dots)$ = F; (D) ${\sim}(Q \leftrightarrow  (P \wedge  R))$ = ${\sim}(T \leftrightarrow  F)$ = T. So (A), (D) are out.
Take $P=F,\ R=T,\ Q=T$: the statement is $F \leftrightarrow  T$ = F, so the negation is T.
(B): ${\sim}(F) \leftrightarrow  T$ = $T \leftrightarrow  T$ = T. (C): ${\sim}P \wedge  (Q \leftrightarrow  {\sim}R)$ = $T \wedge  (T \leftrightarrow  F)$ = F. So (C) is out.
Only (B) survives. Answer: (B).

useful_results: ${\sim}(X \leftrightarrow  Y) \equiv  X \leftrightarrow  {\sim}Y \equiv  {\sim}X \leftrightarrow  Y \equiv  (X \wedge  {\sim}Y) \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y)$.
Translate English carefully: 'dishonest' is ${\sim}R$; 'A and B if and only if C' is $(A \wedge  B) \leftrightarrow  C$.
Two well-chosen test assignments usually eliminate all wrong options in an equivalence MCQ.

questions.question: The only statement among the following that is a tautology is
questions.key_idea: Option (D) is the rule of inference 'modus ponens': $A$ and $A\to  B$ together force $B$.
solution: Truth table in the order $(A,B)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF.
$A \to  B$ = T, F, T, T, and $A \wedge  (A \to  B)$ = T, F, F, F.
(D): $[A \wedge  (A \to  B)] \to  B$ = T, T, T, T. Every value is true, so (D) is a tautology.
(A): $B \to  [A \wedge  (A \to  B)]$ = T, T, F, T. The row FT is false, not a tautology.
(C): $A \vee  (A \wedge  B)$ = T, T, F, F, which equals $A$ (absorption), not a tautology.
(B): $A \wedge  (A \vee  B)$ = T, T, F, F, again equal to $A$ (absorption), not a tautology.
Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Modus ponens: if the premise $A\wedge (A\to  B)$ is true, then $A$ and $A\to  B$ are both true, which forces $B$ true.
solution: An implication $X \to  B$ is a tautology iff $X$ true never goes with $B$ false.
For (D), $X=A \wedge  (A \to  B)$. If $X$ is true then $A$ is true and $A\to  B$ is true, so $B$ is true. Hence (D) can never be false.
By absorption $A \wedge  (A \vee  B) \equiv  A$ and $A \vee  (A \wedge  B) \equiv  A$; a lone $A$ is false when $A=F$, so (B), (C) fail.
For (A): $A=F,\ B=T$ makes $A \wedge  (A\to  B)$ false while $B$ is true, so $B \to  [\dots]$ is false.
Answer: (D).

useful_results: Modus ponens $[A \wedge  (A \to  B)] \to  B$ and modus tollens $[(A \to  B) \wedge  {\sim}B] \to  {\sim}A$ are tautologies.
Absorption: $A \wedge  (A \vee  B) \equiv  A \equiv  A \vee  (A \wedge  B)$.
Hypothetical syllogism $[(A \to  B) \wedge  (B \to  C)] \to  (A \to  C)$ is also a tautology.
Test an implication tautology by trying to make the left side true and the right side false.

questions.question: The negation of the statement 'If I become a teacher, then I will open a school' is
options: I will not become a teacher or I will open a school
I will become a teacher and I will not open a school
Either I will not become a teacher or I will not open a school
Neither I will become a teacher nor I will open a school
questions.answer: (B) I will become a teacher and I will not open a school
questions.key_idea: ${\sim}(p \to  q) \equiv  p \wedge  {\sim}q$: the only way a promise 'if $p$ then $q$' fails is $p$ true and $q$ false.
solution: Let $p$: I become a teacher; $q$: I will open a school. The statement is $p \to  q$.
Its negation is ${\sim}(p \to  q) \equiv  {\sim}({\sim}p \vee  q)$.
By De Morgan: ${\sim}({\sim}p \vee  q) \equiv  p \wedge  {\sim}q$.
In words: I will become a teacher and I will not open a school.
Answer: (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: A conditional fails in exactly one row, $p=T,\ q=F$; find the option true only in that row.
solution: $p \to  q$ is false only for $p=T,\ q=F$, so its negation is true only for that row.
(A) ${\sim}p \vee  q$ is the conditional itself (true in three rows). (C) ${\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q$ is true in three rows. (D) ${\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q$ is true only for $p=F,q=F$.
(B) $p \wedge  {\sim}q$ is true only for $p=T,\ q=F$: the required row.
Answer: (B).

useful_results: ${\sim}(p \to  q) \equiv  p \wedge  {\sim}q$, so a counter-example to 'if $p$ then $q$' is a case with $p$ true and $q$ false.
De Morgan: ${\sim}(p \wedge  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q$, ${\sim}(p \vee  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q$.
'Neither ... nor' is ${\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q$, whereas 'not both' is ${\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q$.

questions.question:
Consider:
Statement-1: $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \wedge  ({\sim}p \wedge  q)$ is a fallacy.
Statement-2: $(p \to  q) \leftrightarrow  ({\sim}q \to  {\sim}p)$ is a tautology.
options: Statement-1 is true, Statement-2 is true; Statement-2 is a correct explanation for Statement-1.
Statement-1 is true, Statement-2 is true; Statement-2 is not a correct explanation for Statement-1.
Statement-1 is true; Statement-2 is false.
Statement-1 is false, Statement-2 is true.
questions.key_idea: A conjunction containing both $p$ and ${\sim}p$ is a fallacy; ${\sim}q\to {\sim}p$ is the contrapositive of $p\to  q$.
solution: Statement-1: $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \wedge  ({\sim}p \wedge  q) = p \wedge  {\sim}q \wedge  {\sim}p \wedge  q$.
Regroup: $= (p \wedge  {\sim}p) \wedge  ({\sim}q \wedge  q)$.
$p \wedge  {\sim}p \equiv  \mathrm{c}$ and ${\sim}q \wedge  q \equiv  \mathrm{c}$, so the statement is $\mathrm{c} \wedge  \mathrm{c} \equiv  \mathrm{c}$ (always false).
Hence it is a fallacy: Statement-1 is true.
Statement-2: ${\sim}q \to  {\sim}p \equiv  q \vee  {\sim}p \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q \equiv  p \to  q$ (the contrapositive).
So Statement-2 is $(p \to  q) \leftrightarrow  (p \to  q)$, which is always true: Statement-2 is true.
The two statements are unrelated facts, so Statement-2 does not explain Statement-1.
Answer: (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Argue with the truth values themselves: the two conjuncts of Statement-1 demand $p$ and ${\sim}p$ simultaneously.
solution: $p \wedge  {\sim}q$ is true only when $p=T$ (and $q=F$); ${\sim}p \wedge  q$ is true only when $p=F$ (and $q=T$).
No assignment makes both true, so Statement-1 is a fallacy.
$p \to  q$ is false only for $(p,q)=(T,F)$. ${\sim}q \to  {\sim}p$ is false only when ${\sim}q=T$ and ${\sim}p=F$, i.e. $q=F,\ p=T$: the same single row.
Two statements false in exactly the same row are equivalent, so their biconditional is true in all rows: Statement-2 is a tautology.
Answer: (B).

useful_results: The contrapositive ${\sim}q \to  {\sim}p$ is always equivalent to $p \to  q$; the converse $q\to  p$ and inverse ${\sim}p \to  {\sim}q$ are equivalent to each other but not to $p\to  q$.
$X \wedge  {\sim}X$ is a fallacy (always false); $X \vee  {\sim}X$ is a tautology.
Two statements are equivalent iff they are false in exactly the same rows.

questions.question: The statement ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$ is
questions.key_idea: Negating one side of a biconditional negates it; negating it twice returns $p\leftrightarrow  q$.
solution: Truth table in the order $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF.
${\sim}q$ = F, T, F, T and $p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q$ = F, T, T, F.
${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$ = T, F, F, T.
$p \leftrightarrow  q$ = T, F, F, T, identical to the column of ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)$.
${\sim}p \leftrightarrow  q$ = F, T, T, F, which differs, so (D) is false; the column has both T and F, so (A), (B) are false.
Answer: (C).
questions.source_note: PDF's last line reads '(p ~ q)'; the bar over the whole expression is lost in print. Read as ~(p <-> ~q).

alternate_solutions.idea: A biconditional is true iff the two sides agree, so work with the 'disagree' reading.
solution: $p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q$ says $p$ and $q$ disagree; its negation says they agree.
'They agree' is exactly $p \leftrightarrow  q$, so (C) holds.
Since $p \leftrightarrow  q$ is false for $p=T,\ q=F$ and true for $p=q=T$, the statement is neither a tautology nor a fallacy.
${\sim}p \leftrightarrow  q$ says $p$ and $q$ disagree, which is the opposite of $p \leftrightarrow  q$: (D) is false.
Answer: (C).

useful_results: ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q) \equiv  p \leftrightarrow  q$ and ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \leftrightarrow  q \equiv  p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q$.
$p \leftrightarrow  q$ is true iff $p,q$ have the same truth value; its negation is the exclusive OR.
A statement that takes both values is neither a tautology nor a fallacy (it is a contingency).

concepts: Negation and simplification of compound statements
questions.question: The negation of ${\sim}s \vee  ({\sim}r \wedge  s)$ is equivalent to
questions.key_idea: Apply De Morgan twice and use $s \wedge  {\sim}s \equiv  \mathrm{c}$ to kill the contradiction.
solution: Negation: ${\sim}({\sim}s \vee  ({\sim}r \wedge  s))$.
De Morgan: $= s \wedge  {\sim}(({\sim}r) \wedge  s)$.
Again: $= s \wedge  (r \vee  ({\sim}s))$.
Distribute: $= (s \wedge  r) \vee  (s \wedge  ({\sim}s))$.
$s \wedge  {\sim}s \equiv  \mathrm{c}$, so $= (s \wedge  r) \vee  \mathrm{c}$.
$X \vee  \mathrm{c} \equiv  X$, so the negation is $s \wedge  r$.
Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: A disjunction is false in exactly one way; find the rows where ${\sim}s \vee  ({\sim}r \wedge  s)$ is false.
solution: ${\sim}s \vee  ({\sim}r \wedge  s)$ is false only when both parts are false.
${\sim}s$ false means $s=T$. Then ${\sim}r \wedge  s$ false means ${\sim}r$ false, i.e. $r=T$.
So the given statement is false only for $s=T,\ r=T$, hence its negation is true only for $s=T,\ r=T$.
That is exactly $s \wedge  r$. Answer: (D).

useful_results: $X \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y) \equiv  X \vee  Y$ and $X \wedge  ({\sim}X \vee  Y) \equiv  X \wedge  Y$ (the negated term is redundant).
Here ${\sim}s \vee  ({\sim}r \wedge  s) \equiv  {\sim}s \vee  {\sim}r \equiv  {\sim}(s \wedge  r)$.
A disjunction is false only when every disjunct is false; a conjunction is true only when every conjunct is true.

questions.question: The Boolean expression $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  q \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  q)$ is equivalent to
questions.key_idea: Distribute $(p \wedge  {\sim}q)\vee  q$ into $(p\vee  q)\wedge ({\sim}q \vee  q)$ and drop the tautology factor.
solution: $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  q \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  q) \equiv  [(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  q] \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  q)$.
Distribute: $[(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  q] \equiv  (p \vee  q) \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  q)$.
${\sim}q \vee  q \equiv  \mathrm{t}$, so $[(p\vee  q) \wedge  \mathrm{t}] \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  q) \equiv  (p \vee  q) \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  q)$.
Distribute again: $(p \vee  q) \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  q) \equiv  (p \vee  q \vee  {\sim}p) \wedge  (p \vee  q \vee  q)$.
$p \vee  q \vee  {\sim}p \equiv  \mathrm{t}$ and $p \vee  q \vee  q \equiv  p \vee  q$.
So the expression is $\mathrm{t} \wedge  (p \vee  q) \equiv  p \vee  q$.
Answer: (A).
questions.source_note: PDF's step '(q v t)' for 'p v q v ~p' is a shorthand (q v t = t); written out here.

alternate_solutions.idea: The expression is a disjunction, so it is false only when every disjunct is false: solve for that single row.
solution: The expression is false iff $p \wedge  {\sim}q$, $q$ and ${\sim}p \wedge  q$ are all false.
$q$ false means $q=F$. Then $p \wedge  {\sim}q$ reduces to $p$, which must be false: $p=F$.
With $p=q=F$, ${\sim}p \wedge  q$ is false as well, so all three disjuncts are false: the expression is false exactly for $p=q=F$.
$p \vee  q$ is false exactly for $p=q=F$, so they are equivalent. Answer: (A).

useful_results: A disjunction of terms is false in exactly the rows where every term is false: list those rows to identify the expression.
$(X \wedge  {\sim}Y) \vee  Y \equiv  X \vee  Y$ and $({\sim}X \wedge  Y) \vee  X \equiv  X \vee  Y$.

questions.question: The following statement $(p \to  q) \to  [({\sim}p \to  q) \to  q]$ is
questions.key_idea: $({\sim}p\to  q)\to  q$ simplifies to $p\to  q$, so the whole statement is $(p\to  q)\to (p\to  q)$.
solution: Truth table, rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF.
$p \to  q$ = T, F, T, T.
${\sim}p$ = F, F, T, T and ${\sim}p \to  q$ = T, T, T, F.
$({\sim}p \to  q) \to  q$ = T, F, T, T.
$(p \to  q) \to  [({\sim}p \to  q) \to  q]$ = T, T, T, T (T\to  T, F\to  F, T\to  T, T\to  T).
All four values are T, so the statement is a tautology.
Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Simplify the inner part algebraically: the statement becomes $X \to  X$.
solution: ${\sim}p \to  q \equiv  p \vee  q$, so $({\sim}p \to  q) \to  q \equiv  (p \vee  q) \to  q \equiv  {\sim}(p \vee  q) \vee  q \equiv  ({\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  q$.
Distribute: $({\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  q \equiv  ({\sim}p \vee  q) \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q \equiv  p \to  q$.
So the statement is $(p \to  q) \to  (p \to  q)$, which has the form $X \to  X$.
$X \to  X \equiv  {\sim}X \vee  X \equiv  \mathrm{t}$: a tautology. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $X \to  X$ is a tautology for every statement $X$.
$({\sim}p \to  q) \to  q \equiv  p \to  q$ (proof by cases on $p$).
$(A \to  B) \to  B \equiv  A \vee  B$; with $A={\sim}p,\ B=q$ this gives ${\sim}p \vee  q \equiv  p \to  q$, as used above.

${\sim}(p \vee  q) \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  q)$ = F, F, T, T.
This column is the same as ${\sim}p$ = F, F, T, T.

solution: ${\sim}(p \vee  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q$.
So the expression is $({\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  q)$.
Factor: ${\sim}p \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \wedge  \mathrm{t}$.

questions.question: The statement among the following that is a tautology is
questions.key_idea: $A\wedge (A\to  B)$ is just $A\wedge  B$, and $(A\wedge  B)\to  B$ always holds.
solution: Truth table, rows $(A,B)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF.
$A \wedge  B$ = T, F, F, F and $A \vee  B$ = T, T, T, F.
(A) $A \vee  (A \wedge  B)$ = T, T, F, F: not a tautology. (C) $A \wedge  (A \vee  B)$ = T, T, F, F: not a tautology.
$A \to  B$ = T, F, T, T and $A \wedge  (A \to  B)$ = T, F, F, F.
(B) $B \to  [A \wedge  (A \to  B)]$ = T, T, F, T: the third row is F, not a tautology.
(D) $[A \wedge  (A \to  B)] \to  B$ = T, T, T, T: a tautology.
Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Simplify $A \wedge  (A \to  B)$ to $A \wedge  B$; then (D) is 'a conjunction implies its conjunct'.
solution: $A \wedge  (A \to  B) \equiv  A \wedge  ({\sim}A \vee  B) \equiv  (A \wedge  {\sim}A) \vee  (A \wedge  B) \equiv  A \wedge  B$.
So (D) is $(A \wedge  B) \to  B \equiv  {\sim}(A \wedge  B) \vee  B \equiv  {\sim}A \vee  {\sim}B \vee  B$.
${\sim}B \vee  B \equiv  \mathrm{t}$, so (D) is a tautology.
The others fail: (A), (C) both equal $A$ (absorption), false at $A=F$; (B) is false at $A=F,\ B=T$.
Answer: (D).

useful_results: $A \wedge  (A \to  B) \equiv  A \wedge  B$ and $A \vee  (A \wedge  {\sim}B) \equiv  A$.
$(A \wedge  B) \to  A$ and $(A \wedge  B) \to  B$ (simplification) are tautologies, as is $A \to  (A \vee  B)$ (addition).
Absorption: $A \vee  (A \wedge  B) \equiv  A \wedge  (A \vee  B) \equiv  A$.

questions.question: The negation of the statement ${\sim}p \wedge  (p \vee  q)$ is
questions.key_idea: De Morgan, then $p\vee ({\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q)$ becomes $(p\vee {\sim}p)\wedge (p\vee {\sim}q)$.
solution: ${\sim}({\sim}p \wedge  (p \vee  q)) \equiv  p \vee  {\sim}(p \vee  q)$.
${\sim}(p \vee  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q$, so this is $p \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q)$.
Distribute: $(p \vee  {\sim}p) \wedge  (p \vee  {\sim}q)$.
$p \vee  {\sim}p \equiv  \mathrm{t}$, so the result is $\mathrm{t} \wedge  (p \vee  {\sim}q)$.
$= p \vee  {\sim}q$.
Answer: (D).

solution: ${\sim}p \wedge  (p \vee  q) \equiv  ({\sim}p \wedge  p) \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  q) \equiv  \mathrm{c} \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \wedge  q$.
Negation of ${\sim}p \wedge  q$ by De Morgan is $p \vee  {\sim}q$.
Answer: (D).

useful_results: ${\sim}p \wedge  (p \vee  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \wedge  q$ (the term $p$ inside is redundant next to ${\sim}p$).
${\sim}({\sim}p \wedge  q) \equiv  p \vee  {\sim}q$; ${\sim}(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q$.
$X \wedge  ({\sim}X \vee  Y) \equiv  X \wedge  Y$ and $X \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y) \equiv  X \vee  Y$.

questions.question:
For the statements $p$ and $q$, consider the following compound statements:
(a) $({\sim}q \wedge  (p \to  q)) \to  {\sim}p$
(b) $((p \vee  q) \wedge  {\sim}p) \to  q$
Then which of the following statements is correct?
questions.key_idea: (a) is modus tollens and (b) is disjunctive syllogism; both are valid arguments, hence tautologies.
solution: (a): $({\sim}q \wedge  (p \to  q)) \to  {\sim}p \equiv  {\sim}({\sim}q \wedge  (p \to  q)) \vee  {\sim}p$.
$= (q \vee  {\sim}(p \to  q)) \vee  {\sim}p = (q \vee  (p \wedge  {\sim}q)) \vee  {\sim}p$.
Distribute: $q \vee  (p \wedge  {\sim}q) \equiv  (q \vee  p) \wedge  (q \vee  {\sim}q) \equiv  (q \vee  p) \wedge  \mathrm{t}$.
So (a) $= (q \vee  p) \vee  {\sim}p = q \vee  (p \vee  {\sim}p) = q \vee  \mathrm{t} = \mathrm{t}$: a tautology.
(b): $((p \vee  q) \wedge  {\sim}p) \to  q \equiv  {\sim}((p \vee  q) \wedge  {\sim}p) \vee  q = ({\sim}(p \vee  q) \vee  p) \vee  q$.
${\sim}(p \vee  q) \vee  p = ({\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  p = ({\sim}p \vee  p) \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  p) = \mathrm{t} \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  p) = p \vee  {\sim}q$.
So (b) $= p \vee  {\sim}q \vee  q = p \vee  ({\sim}q \vee  q) = p \vee  \mathrm{t} = \mathrm{t}$: a tautology.
Both are tautologies. Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Argue by falsifying assignments: each statement is an implication, so look for premise true and conclusion false.
solution: (a) is false only if ${\sim}p$ is false ($p=T$) while ${\sim}q \wedge  (p \to  q)$ is true.
With $p=T$: $p \to  q$ true forces $q=T$, but then ${\sim}q$ is false, so the premise is false. No falsifying row: (a) is a tautology.
(b) is false only if $q=F$ while $(p \vee  q) \wedge  {\sim}p$ is true.
With $q=F$: $p \vee  q$ true forces $p=T$, but then ${\sim}p$ is false, so the premise fails. No falsifying row: (b) is a tautology.
Answer: (D).

useful_results: Modus tollens: $[(p \to  q) \wedge  {\sim}q] \to  {\sim}p$ is a tautology.
Disjunctive syllogism: $[(p \vee  q) \wedge  {\sim}p] \to  q$ is a tautology.
Valid argument forms (modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, disjunctive syllogism) are exactly tautologies of the form premises $\to$ conclusion.

questions.question: The statement $A \to  (B \to  A)$ is equivalent to
questions.key_idea: $A\to (B\to  A)$ is a tautology, so the equivalent option is the only tautologous one.
solution: $A \to  (B \to  A) \equiv  {\sim}A \vee  (B \to  A)$.
$\equiv  {\sim}A \vee  ({\sim}B \vee  A) \equiv  ({\sim}A \vee  A) \vee  {\sim}B$.
${\sim}A \vee  A \equiv  \mathrm{t}$ and $\mathrm{t} \vee  {\sim}B \equiv  \mathrm{t}$, so the statement is a tautology.
(A): $A \to  (A \vee  B) \equiv  {\sim}A \vee  (A \vee  B) \equiv  ({\sim}A \vee  A) \vee  B \equiv  \mathrm{t}$: a tautology, hence equivalent to the given statement.
(B): $A \to  (A \to  B) \equiv  {\sim}A \vee  ({\sim}A \vee  B) \equiv  {\sim}A \vee  B$, not a tautology (false at $A=T,\ B=F$).
(C): for $A=T$, $A \leftrightarrow  B$ is $B$, so $A \to  (A \leftrightarrow  B) \equiv  {\sim}A \vee  B$ (false at $A=T,\ B=F$).
(D): $A \to  (A \wedge  B) \equiv  {\sim}A \vee  (A \wedge  B) \equiv  ({\sim}A \vee  A) \wedge  ({\sim}A \vee  B) \equiv  {\sim}A \vee  B$, not a tautology.
Only (A) is a tautology. Answer: (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Exportation: $A \to  (B \to  A) \equiv  (A \wedge  B) \to  A$, which is the simple fact that a conjunction implies its conjunct.
solution: Exportation law: $X \to  (Y \to  Z) \equiv  (X \wedge  Y) \to  Z$.
So $A \to  (B \to  A) \equiv  (A \wedge  B) \to  A$.
If $A \wedge  B$ is true then $A$ is true, so this implication can never be false: a tautology.
Among the options, only $A \to  (A \vee  B)$ is also a tautology (if $A$ is true, $A \vee  B$ is true).
The other three equal ${\sim}A \vee  B$, false at $A=T,\ B=F$. Answer: (A).

useful_results: Exportation: $X \to  (Y \to  Z) \equiv  (X \wedge  Y) \to  Z$; in particular $A \to  (A \to  B) \equiv  A \to  B$.
$A \to  (A \wedge  B) \equiv  A \to  B$ and $A \to  (A \leftrightarrow  B) \equiv  A \to  B$ (the leading $A$ makes the second $A$ true).
$A \to  (A \vee  B)$ and $A \to  (B \to  A)$ are tautologies.

questions.question: The contrapositive of the statement 'If you will work, you will earn money' is
options: If you will earn money, you will work
To earn money, you need to work
If you will not earn money, you will not work
You will earn money, if you will not work
questions.answer: (C) If you will not earn money, you will not work
questions.key_idea: The contrapositive of $p\to  q$ is ${\sim}q \to  {\sim}p$ (negate and swap).
solution: Let $p$: you will work; $q$: you will earn money.
The statement is $p \to  q$.
Its contrapositive is ${\sim}q \to  {\sim}p$.
In words: if you will not earn money, you will not work.
(A) and (B) say $q \to  p$ (the converse); (D) says ${\sim}p \to  q$. Neither is the contrapositive.
Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Think of who breaks each promise: an equivalent statement must be broken by exactly the same people.
solution: 'If you work you earn money' is broken only by someone who works but earns nothing.
(C) 'if you do not earn, you do not work' is broken only by someone who earns nothing but works: the same person.
(A) is broken by someone who earns but does not work, which does not break the original: not equivalent.
(D) is broken by someone who does not work and earns nothing: not equivalent either. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $p \to  q \equiv  {\sim}q \to  {\sim}p$ (contrapositive); the converse $q \to  p$ and the inverse ${\sim}p \to  {\sim}q$ are equivalent to each other but not to $p \to  q$.
'$q$ is necessary for $p$' means $p \to  q$; so 'to earn money you need to work' is $q \to  p$, not the given statement.

$F_1$ is a tautology but $F_2$ is not a tautology

solution: Tabulate $F_1$ over the 8 rows $(A,B,C)$ = TTT, TFF, TTF, TFT, FTT, FFF, FTF, FFT.
$A \wedge  {\sim}B$ = F, T, F, T, F, F, F, F and ${\sim}A$ = F, F, F, F, T, T, T, T.

$F_2$: $B \to  {\sim}A \equiv  {\sim}B \vee  {\sim}A$, so $F_2 = A \vee  B \vee  {\sim}B \vee  {\sim}A$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A disjunction is false only if all disjuncts are false: solve for the single falsifying row of $F_1$ directly.
solution: $F_1$ is false iff ${\sim}A$, $A \wedge  {\sim}B$ and ${\sim}C \wedge  (A \vee  B)$ are all false.

So $F_1$ is false at $A=B=C=T$: not a tautology.
$F_2$: $B \to  {\sim}A \equiv  {\sim}B \vee  {\sim}A$ so $F_2$ contains both $A$ and ${\sim}A$ as disjuncts: always true. Answer: (A).

To refute a tautology claim for a disjunction, force every disjunct false and solve successively (here $A=B=C=T$).
$B \to  {\sim}A \equiv  {\sim}(A \wedge  B)$ (NAND).

questions.question: If $P$ and $Q$ are two statements, then which of the following compound statements is a tautology?
questions.key_idea: $((P\to  Q)\wedge {\sim}Q)\to {\sim}P$ is modus tollens.
solution: Truth table, rows $(P,Q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF.
${\sim}P$ = F, F, T, T and ${\sim}Q$ = F, T, F, T.
$P \to  Q$ = T, F, T, T.
$(P \to  Q) \wedge  {\sim}Q$ = F, F, F, T.
$((P \to  Q) \wedge  {\sim}Q) \to  {\sim}P$ = T, T, T, T (in the only true-premise row FF, ${\sim}P$ is T).
So option (C) is a tautology (modus tollens).
(A): at $P=Q=F$ the premise is T and $Q$ is F, so it is false. (B): at $P=Q=F$, $P \wedge  Q$ is F, so it is false.
Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Modus tollens in words: if the premise holds, $P$ cannot be true, because $P$ would force $Q$ against ${\sim}Q$.
solution: Suppose $(P \to  Q) \wedge  {\sim}Q$ is true. Then ${\sim}Q$ is true, so $Q$ is false.
If $P$ were true, $P \to  Q$ would make $Q$ true: a contradiction. Hence $P$ is false, i.e. ${\sim}P$ is true.
So whenever the premise is true the conclusion ${\sim}P$ is true: the implication is a tautology.
For (A) and (B) the premise forces $P=Q=F$ and then $Q$, $P\wedge  Q$ are false. Answer: (C).

useful_results: Modus tollens: $[(P \to  Q) \wedge  {\sim}Q] \to  {\sim}P$ is a tautology.

Rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF: $p \wedge  q$ = T, F, F, F and $p \to  q$ = T, F, T, T.

questions.question: If the Boolean expression $(p \to  q) \leftrightarrow  (q * ({\sim}p))$ is a tautology, then the Boolean expression $p * ({\sim}q)$ is equivalent to
questions.key_idea: $p\to  q \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q$, so $*$ must be $\vee$; then $p*({\sim}q)=p\vee {\sim}q$ is $q\to  p$.
solution: A tautology $X \leftrightarrow  Y$ means $X \equiv  Y$, so $q * ({\sim}p) \equiv  p \to  q$.
$p \to  q \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q \equiv  q \vee  {\sim}p$, so $*$ is $\vee$.
Check by table, rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF: $p \to  q$ = T, F, T, T and $q \vee  {\sim}p$ = T, F, T, T. They agree.
Other connectives fail: for $p=q=T$, $q \wedge  {\sim}p$, $q \to  {\sim}p$ and $q \leftrightarrow  {\sim}p$ are all F while $p \to  q$ is T.
Hence $* = \vee$ and $p * ({\sim}q) = p \vee  {\sim}q$.
$p \vee  {\sim}q \equiv  {\sim}q \vee  p \equiv  q \to  p$.
Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Read the truth table of $*$ off the tautology condition instead of guessing it.

Row $(p,q)=(T,T)$: $(x,y)=(T,F)$ and $p\to  q=T$, so $T*F=T$.
Row $(T,F)$: $(x,y)=(F,F)$ and $p\to  q=F$, so $F*F=F$.
Row $(F,T)$: $(x,y)=(T,T)$, value $T$, so $T*T=T$. Row $(F,F)$: $(x,y)=(F,T)$, value $T$, so $F*T=T$.
The table T,T,T,F for TT, TF, FT, FF is that of OR, so $* = \vee$ and $p * {\sim}q = p \vee  {\sim}q \equiv  q \to  p$. Answer: (C).

questions.question: Which of the following Boolean expressions is a tautology?
questions.key_idea: Only (C) is guaranteed true: $p\wedge  q$ true makes $p\to  q$ true.
solution: (A): $(p \wedge  q) \vee  (p \vee  q) \equiv  p \vee  q$, false when $p=q=F$. Not a tautology.
(B): $p \to  q \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q$, and $(p \wedge  q) \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  q) \equiv  p \wedge  q$ (since $p\wedge ({\sim}p\vee  q) \equiv  p\wedge  q$); false at $p=F$. Not a tautology.
(C): $(p \wedge  q) \to  (p \to  q) \equiv  {\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  (p \to  q)$.
$= ({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q) \vee  ({\sim}p \vee  q) \equiv  ({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}p) \vee  ({\sim}q \vee  q)$.
$= {\sim}p \vee  \mathrm{t} \equiv  \mathrm{t}$. So (C) is a tautology.
(D): $(p \wedge  q) \vee  ({\sim}p \vee  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q$ (as $p\wedge  q$ is absorbed), false at $p=T,\ q=F$. Not a tautology.
Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Falsifier search: an implication fails only when the premise is true and the conclusion false.
solution: (C) can fail only if $p \wedge  q$ is true and $p \to  q$ is false.
$p \wedge  q$ true means $p=q=T$, and then $p \to  q$ is true. So (C) never fails: a tautology.
The other three are false in some row: (A) at $p=q=F$; (B) at $p=F$ (as $p\wedge  q$ is false); (D) at $p=T,\ q=F$. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $(p \wedge  q) \to  X$ is a tautology for every $X$ implied by $p\wedge  q$ ($p$, $q$, $p\vee  q$, $p\to  q$, $p\leftrightarrow  q$).
$(p \wedge  q) \wedge  (p \to  q) \equiv  p \wedge  q$ and $(p \wedge  q) \vee  (p \to  q) \equiv  p \to  q$.
A conjunction is a tautology only if all conjuncts are; a conjunction with $p\wedge  q$ cannot be.

questions.question: The Boolean expression $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \to  (q \vee  {\sim}p)$ is equivalent to
questions.key_idea: Replace the conditional by ${\sim}(\cdot)\vee (\cdot)$; the ${\sim}p$ and $q$ terms repeat.
solution: $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \to  (q \vee  {\sim}p) \equiv  {\sim}(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  (q \vee  {\sim}p)$.
De Morgan: $= ({\sim}p \vee  q) \vee  (q \vee  {\sim}p)$.
Regroup: $= ({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}p) \vee  (q \vee  q)$.
$= {\sim}p \vee  q$.
${\sim}p \vee  q \equiv  p \to  q$.
Answer: (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: The conditional is false only when its premise is true and its conclusion false: find that single row.
solution: The expression is false iff $p \wedge  {\sim}q$ is true and $q \vee  {\sim}p$ is false.
$p \wedge  {\sim}q$ true: $p=T,\ q=F$. Then $q \vee  {\sim}p = F \vee  F = F$, so the conclusion is indeed false.
So the expression is false only at $p=T,\ q=F$.
That is also the only falsifying row of $p \to  q$. Answer: (B).

useful_results: ${\sim}(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \equiv  p \to  q$; $p \to  q \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q$.

$(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \to  (q \vee  {\sim}p)$ has the form ${\sim}X \to  X$ with $X=p\to  q$, and ${\sim}X \to  X \equiv  X \vee  X \equiv  X$ (here ${\sim}X \equiv  p\wedge {\sim}q$ and $X \equiv  q\vee {\sim}p$).
${\sim}X \to  Y \equiv  X \vee  Y$ and $X \to  Y \equiv  {\sim}Y \to  {\sim}X$.

questions.question:
Consider the following three statements:
(A) If $3+3=7$ then $4+3=8$.
(B) If $5+3=8$ then earth is flat.
(C) If both (A) and (B) are true then $5+6=17$.
Then, which of the following statements is correct?
options: (A) is false, but (B) and (C) are true
(A) is true while (B) and (C) are false
(A) and (C) are true while (B) is false
(A) and (B) are false while (C) is true
questions.key_idea: $p\to  q$ is false only for $p$ true and $q$ false; a false premise makes the conditional true.
solution: Recall: $p \to  q$ is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false.
(A): premise $3+3=7$ is false, so (A) is true.
(B): premise $5+3=8$ is true and conclusion 'earth is flat' is false, so (B) is false.
(C): the premise '(A) and (B) are both true' is false (since (B) is false), so (C) is true.
So (A) is true, (B) is false, (C) is true.
Answer: (C).
questions.source_note: PDF shows only the truth table of p->q and the verdicts 'A true, B false, C true'; the three evaluations are written out.
useful_results: A conditional with a false premise is true (vacuous truth); it is false only for (true premise, false conclusion).
Evaluate nested statements from the inside out: decide $A$ and $B$ first, then $C$.
The truth of $p\to  q$ has nothing to do with any 'cause' linking $p$ and $q$.

questions.question: Which of the following Boolean expressions is not a tautology?
questions.key_idea: Convert each $X\to  Y$ to ${\sim}X\vee  Y$ and look for a complementary pair.
solution: (A): $(q \to  p) \vee  ({\sim}q \to  p) \equiv  ({\sim}q \vee  p) \vee  (q \vee  p)$.
$= ({\sim}q \vee  q) \vee  (p \vee  p) = \mathrm{t} \vee  p = \mathrm{t}$: tautology.
(B): $(p \to  {\sim}q) \vee  ({\sim}q \to  p) \equiv  ({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q) \vee  (q \vee  p)$.
$= (p \vee  {\sim}p) \vee  (q \vee  {\sim}q) = \mathrm{t} \vee  \mathrm{t} = \mathrm{t}$: tautology.
(C): $({\sim}p \to  q) \vee  ({\sim}q \to  p) \equiv  (p \vee  q) \vee  (q \vee  p) = (p \vee  p) \vee  (q \vee  q) = p \vee  q$.
$p \vee  q$ is false at $p=q=F$, so (C) is not a tautology.
(D): $(p \to  q) \vee  ({\sim}q \to  p) \equiv  ({\sim}p \vee  q) \vee  (q \vee  p) = ({\sim}p \vee  p) \vee  q = \mathrm{t} \vee  q = \mathrm{t}$: tautology.
Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Case-split on one variable: in each case one of the two disjuncts is automatically true.
solution: (A): if $q=F$ the first disjunct $q \to  p$ is true; if $q=T$ the second disjunct ${\sim}q \to  p$ is true (false premise). Tautology.
(B): if $p=F$, $p \to  {\sim}q$ is true; if $p=T$, ${\sim}q \to  p$ is true (conclusion $p$ is true). Tautology.
(D): if $p=F$, $p \to  q$ is true; if $p=T$, ${\sim}q \to  p$ is true. Tautology.
(C): at $p=q=F$, ${\sim}p \to  q$ is $T \to  F=F$ and ${\sim}q \to  p$ is $T \to  F=F$, so the whole is false.
Answer: (C).

useful_results: $(X \to  Y) \vee  ({\sim}X \to  Y)$ type patterns: $(A \to  B) \vee  (B \to  A)$ is a tautology (any two statements are comparable in one direction).
$({\sim}p \to  q) \vee  ({\sim}q \to  p) \equiv  p \vee  q$ because each conditional is $p \vee  q$ in disguise.
Case-splitting on one variable settles many tautology checks in one line.

questions.question: The Boolean expression $(p \to  q) \wedge  (q \to  {\sim}p)$ is equivalent to
questions.key_idea: If $p$ were true, the two conditionals would force $q$ and ${\sim}q$ together; so the conjunction is true only when $p$ is false.
solution: Truth table, rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF.
${\sim}p$ = F, F, T, T and $p \to  q$ = T, F, T, T.
$q \to  {\sim}p$ = F, T, T, T.
$(p \to  q) \wedge  (q \to  {\sim}p)$ = F, F, T, T.
This column equals that of ${\sim}p$ (F, F, T, T).
Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Case analysis on $p$.
solution: If $p=T$: $p \to  q$ forces $q=T$, but then $q \to  {\sim}p$ has a true premise and false conclusion, so it is false: the conjunction is F.
If $p=F$: both $p \to  q$ and $q \to  {\sim}p$ are true (false premise, true conclusion respectively): the conjunction is T.
The value is T exactly when $p$ is F, i.e. it equals ${\sim}p$. Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Convert to a disjunction and factor.
solution: $({\sim}p \vee  q) \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  {\sim}p)$.
Factor ${\sim}p$: $= {\sim}p \vee  (q \wedge  {\sim}q) = {\sim}p \vee  \mathrm{c} = {\sim}p$. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $(p \to  q) \wedge  (p \to  {\sim}q) \equiv  {\sim}p$: two opposite consequences of $p$ refute $p$ (reductio).
Here $q \to  {\sim}p \equiv  p \to  {\sim}q$ by contraposition, so the expression is $(p\to  q)\wedge (p\to {\sim}q)$.
$(X \vee  Y) \wedge  (X \vee  {\sim}Y) \equiv  X$.

questions.question: Consider the statement 'The match will be played only if the weather is good and ground is not wet'. Select the correct negation from the following:
options: The match will not be played or weather is good and ground is not wet.
The match will be played and weather is not good or ground is wet.
The match will not be played and weather is not good and ground is wet.
If the match will not be played, then either weather is not good or ground is wet.
questions.key_idea: '$p$ only if $r$' is $p\to  r$; its negation is $p \wedge  {\sim}r$, here ${\sim}(q \wedge  r)$ is ${\sim}q \vee  {\sim}r$.
solution: Let $p$: the match will be played; $q$: weather is good; $r$: ground is not wet.
'$p$ only if $(q\wedge  r)$' means $p \to  (q \wedge  r)$, which is ${\sim}p \vee  (q \wedge  r)$.
Negation: ${\sim}[{\sim}p \vee  (q \wedge  r)]$.
De Morgan: $p \wedge  {\sim}(q \wedge  r)$.
De Morgan again: $p \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  {\sim}r)$.
In words: the match will be played and the weather is not good or the ground is wet.
Answer: (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: List the situations in which the promise is broken.
solution: The promise 'played only if (good weather and dry ground)' is broken only when the match is played although the weather is bad or the ground is wet.
That situation is: played, and (weather not good or ground wet): option (B).
(A) contains 'will not be played or ...', which is the promise itself (true when not played). (C) needs both conditions to fail. (D) is again an implication, not a breach.
Answer: (B).

useful_results: '$p$ only if $q$' is $p \to  q$, whereas '$p$ if $q$' is $q \to  p$ and '$p$ if and only if $q$' is $p \leftrightarrow  q$.
${\sim}(p \to  (q \wedge  r)) \equiv  p \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  {\sim}r)$.
A negation of a promise is a breach: the condition happens and the result fails.

questions.question: The compound statement $(P \vee  Q) \wedge  ({\sim}P) \to  Q$ is equivalent to
questions.key_idea: The statement is disjunctive syllogism (a tautology), so it is equivalent to the only tautologous option.
solution: $(P \vee  Q) \wedge  {\sim}P \to  Q$, i.e. $[(P \vee  Q) \wedge  {\sim}P] \to  Q$.
Distribute: $(P \vee  Q) \wedge  {\sim}P = (P \wedge  {\sim}P) \vee  (Q \wedge  {\sim}P) = \mathrm{c} \vee  (Q \wedge  {\sim}P) = Q \wedge  {\sim}P$.
Statement $= (Q \wedge  {\sim}P) \to  Q = {\sim}(Q \wedge  {\sim}P) \vee  Q$.
${\sim}(Q \wedge  {\sim}P) = {\sim}Q \vee  P$, so the statement $= ({\sim}Q \vee  P) \vee  Q = ({\sim}Q \vee  Q) \vee  P$.
$= \mathrm{t} \vee  P = \mathrm{t}$: the statement is a tautology.
Option (A): ${\sim}(P \to  Q) = {\sim}({\sim}P \vee  Q) = P \wedge  {\sim}Q$, so (A) reads $(P \wedge  {\sim}Q) \leftrightarrow  (P \wedge  {\sim}Q)$, a tautology.
(B), (C) are false when $P=F$, and (D) is false when $P=Q=F$; so only (A) is equivalent to a tautology.
Answer: (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Semantic argument: assume the premise holds and deduce the conclusion.
solution: Suppose $(P \vee  Q) \wedge  {\sim}P$ is true. Then ${\sim}P$ is true, so $P=F$.
With $P=F$ the true disjunction $P \vee  Q$ forces $Q=T$.
So whenever the premise is true, $Q$ is true: the implication is a tautology (disjunctive syllogism).
Hence it is equivalent to the only tautologous option, (A), because ${\sim}(P \to  Q) \equiv  P \wedge  {\sim}Q$. Answer: (A).

useful_results: Disjunctive syllogism: $[(P \vee  Q) \wedge  {\sim}P] \to  Q$ is a tautology.
${\sim}(P \to  Q) \equiv  P \wedge  {\sim}Q$, hence ${\sim}(P \to  Q) \leftrightarrow  (P \wedge  {\sim}Q)$ is a tautology.
Every tautology is equivalent to every other tautology, so 'equivalent to' a tautology means 'is itself a tautology'.

questions.question: Which of the following is the negation of the statement 'for all $M>0$, there exists $x \in S$ such that $x \ge M$'?
options: there exists $M>0$ and there exists $x\in S$ such that $x<M$
there exists $M>0$, such that $x<M$ for all $x \in S$
there exists $M>0$ and there exists $x\in S$ such that $x\ge M$
there exists $M>0$, such that $x \ge M$ for all $x\in S$
questions.answer: (B) there exists $M>0$, such that $x<M$ for all $x\in S$
questions.key_idea: Negating swaps each quantifier ($\forall\leftrightarrow\exists$) in turn and negates the final condition $x\ge M$ to $x<M$.
solution: Statement: $\forall M>0\ \ \exists x\in S:\ x\ge M$.
Negation of 'for all $M>0$' is 'there exists $M>0$'.
Negation of 'there exists $x\in S$' is 'for all $x\in S$'.
Negation of $x\ge M$ is $x<M$.
So the negation is: there exists $M>0$ such that $x<M$ for all $x\in S$.
Answer: (B).
questions.source_note: PDF says only 'Negation of for all is there exists. There exists M>0 such that x<M for all x in S'; the quantifier-by-quantifier steps are written out.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the options on two sets $S$ whose truth value for the original statement is known.
solution: Take $S=[0,\infty)$: for each $M>0$ choose $x=M$, so the statement is true and its negation must be false.
For this $S$, (A) and (C) are true (take $M=1,\ x=0$ for (A); $M=1,\ x=1$ for (C)), so (A) and (C) are not the negation.
Take $S=(0,1)$: the statement fails for $M=2$, so its negation must be true.
For this $S$, (D) says some $M>0$ is below every $x\in(0,1)$, false because $x$ can be arbitrarily small; (B) holds with $M=2$. Answer: (B).

useful_results: ${\sim}(\forall M\ \exists x\ P) \equiv  \exists M\ \forall x\ {\sim}P$: negation flips every quantifier and the innermost condition.
The statement 'for all $M>0$ there is $x\in S$ with $x\ge M$' says $S$ is unbounded above; its negation says $S$ is bounded above by some $M$.
Order of quantifiers matters: $\forall M\,\exists x$ and $\exists x\,\forall M$ are different claims.

questions.question: If the truth value of the Boolean expression $((p \vee  q) \wedge  (q \to  r) \wedge  ({\sim}r)) \to  (p \wedge  q)$ is false, then the truth values of the statements $p,\ q,\ r$ respectively can be
questions.key_idea: A conditional is false only if its premise is true and its conclusion false; this fixes $r$, then $q$, then $p$ one by one.
solution: The conditional is false only if $p \wedge  q$ is false and $(p \vee  q) \wedge  (q \to  r) \wedge  {\sim}r$ is true.
${\sim}r$ true gives $r=F$.
$q \to  r$ true with $r=F$ needs ${\sim}q \vee  r$ true, i.e. ${\sim}q$ true, so $q=F$.
$p \vee  q$ true with $q=F$ gives $p=T$.
Check: $p\wedge  q = T\wedge  F = F$, so the conclusion is false, as required.
So $p,q,r$ are T, F, F.
Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute the four options directly and see which makes the premise true while $p\wedge  q$ is false.
solution: (A) $p,q,r=F,T,F$: $q \to  r = T \to  F = F$, so the premise is false and the whole conditional is true. Reject.
(B) $T,F,T$: ${\sim}r=F$, premise false, conditional true. Reject. (C) $F,F,T$: ${\sim}r=F$, premise false. Reject.
(D) $T,F,F$: $p\vee  q=T$, $q\to  r=T$, ${\sim}r=T$, so premise true, while $p\wedge  q=F$: the conditional is false.
Answer: (D).

useful_results: $X \to  Y$ is false in exactly one way: $X$ true and $Y$ false. Setting up the conditions for that single case fixes the truth values.
A conjunction $A \wedge  B \wedge  C$ is true iff each factor is true, so each factor gives a separate condition.
Solve the equations in the order that forces values (${\sim}r$ first).

questions.question:
Consider the two statements:
(S1): $(p \to  q) \vee  ({\sim}q \to  p)$ is a tautology.
(S2): $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  q)$ is a fallacy.
Then:
questions.key_idea: $(S1)$ splits on $p$; $(S2)$ needs $p\wedge {\sim}q$ and ${\sim}p\vee  q$ together, which contradict each other.
solution: Truth table, rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF.
$p \to  q$ = T, F, T, T and ${\sim}q \to  p$ = T, T, T, F.
(S1) $(p \to  q) \vee  ({\sim}q \to  p)$ = T, T, T, T: a tautology, so (S1) is true.
$p \wedge  {\sim}q$ = F, T, F, F and ${\sim}p \vee  q$ = T, F, T, T.
(S2) $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  q)$ = F, F, F, F: always false, a fallacy, so (S2) is true.
Both statements are true. Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Argue by cases rather than a table.
solution: (S1): if $p=F$ then $p \to  q$ is true; if $p=T$ then ${\sim}q \to  p$ is true (conclusion $p$ is true). So the disjunction is always true.
(S2): $p \wedge  {\sim}q$ true forces $p=T,\ q=F$. Then ${\sim}p \vee  q = F \vee  F = F$.
So the two conjuncts are never true together: (S2) is a fallacy. Answer: (D).

useful_results: $(p \to  q) \vee  (q \to  p)$ and $(p \to  q) \vee  ({\sim}q \to  p)$ are tautologies: a disjunction of two conditionals that cover both cases of one variable.
$(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  q) \equiv  \mathrm{c}$ because $p \wedge  {\sim}q \equiv  {\sim}(p \to  q)$ and ${\sim}p \vee  q \equiv  p \to  q$: ${\sim}X \wedge  X \equiv  \mathrm{c}$.
A statement of the form ${\sim}X \wedge  X$ is a fallacy; ${\sim}X \vee  X$ is a tautology.

questions.question: The statement $(p \wedge  (p \to  q) \wedge  (q \to  r)) \to  r$ is
questions.key_idea: It is two successive modus ponens: $p$ and $p\to  q$ give $q$, then $q$ and $q\to  r$ give $r$.
solution: Write the conditionals as disjunctions: $[p \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  q)] \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  r) \to  r$.
Distribute: $p \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  q) = (p \wedge  {\sim}p) \vee  (p \wedge  q) = \mathrm{c} \vee  (p \wedge  q) = p \wedge  q$.
So the premise is $(p \wedge  q) \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  r) = p \wedge  [q \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  r)]$.
$q \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  r) = (q \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  (q \wedge  r) = \mathrm{c} \vee  (q \wedge  r) = q \wedge  r$.
The premise is $p \wedge  q \wedge  r$, and the statement is $(p \wedge  q \wedge  r) \to  r$.
$= {\sim}(p \wedge  q \wedge  r) \vee  r = {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q \vee  {\sim}r \vee  r$.
${\sim}r \vee  r \equiv  \mathrm{t}$, so the whole is $({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q) \vee  \mathrm{t} = \mathrm{t}$: a tautology.
Answer: (D).
