alternate_solutions.idea: Chain of inferences: assume the premise true and derive $r$ (hypothetical syllogism).
solution: Assume $p$, $p \to  q$ and $q \to  r$ are all true.
From $p$ and $p \to  q$ we get $q$ (modus ponens).
From $q$ and $q \to  r$ we get $r$ (modus ponens again).
So whenever the premise is true, $r$ is true: the implication can never be false, a tautology. Answer: (D).

useful_results: Hypothetical syllogism: $[(p \to  q) \wedge  (q \to  r)] \to  (p \to  r)$ is a tautology; with $p$ added, $[p \wedge  (p \to  q) \wedge  (q \to  r)] \to  r$.
A long chain of implications $p\to  q,\ q\to  r,\ r\to  s,\dots$ with $p$ true yields every later statement true.
$X \wedge  ({\sim}X \vee  Y) \equiv  X \wedge  Y$.

questions.question: The Boolean expression $(p \wedge  q) \to  ((r \wedge  q) \wedge  p)$ is equivalent to
questions.key_idea: $X\to (X\wedge  Y)$ is the same as $X\to  Y$; the repeated $p$ and $q$ on the right are redundant.
solution: $(p \wedge  q) \to  ((r \wedge  q) \wedge  p) \equiv  {\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  [(r \wedge  q) \wedge  p]$.
Write $(r \wedge  q) \wedge  p = (r \wedge  q) \wedge  (p \wedge  q)$ (since $q$ already appears).
Distribute: ${\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  [(r \wedge  q) \wedge  (p \wedge  q)] = [{\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  (p \wedge  q)] \wedge  [{\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  (r \wedge  q)]$.
${\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  (p \wedge  q) \equiv  \mathrm{t}$, so the expression is $\mathrm{t} \wedge  [{\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  (r \wedge  q)]$.
$= {\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  (r \wedge  q) \equiv  (p \wedge  q) \to  (r \wedge  q)$.
Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Both sides are conditionals with the same premise $p\wedge  q$, so compare them only in the rows where $p=q=T$.
solution: The expression is false iff $p=q=T$ and $(r \wedge  q) \wedge  p$ is false, i.e. $r=F$. So it is false only at $(p,q,r)=(T,T,F)$.
(D) is false iff $p=q=T$ and $r \wedge  q$ is false, i.e. $r=F$: the same single row.
(A) is false at $(p,q,r)=(F,T,T)$, (B) is a tautology ($q$ is true when $p\wedge  q$ is), (C) is false at $(T,F,T)$: none matches.
Answer: (D).

useful_results: $X \to  (X \wedge  Y) \equiv  X \to  Y$: the premise can be repeated for free in the conclusion.
Under the premise $p\wedge  q$ the statements $p$ and $q$ are both true, so they can be inserted into or deleted from the conclusion.
Two conditionals with the same premise are equivalent iff their conclusions agree wherever the premise is true.

questions.question: Let $*,\ \square \in \{\wedge ,\ \vee \}$ be such that the Boolean expression $(p * {\sim}q) \to  (p \square q)$ is a tautology. Then:
questions.key_idea: Check the four combinations; $p\wedge {\sim}q$ implies $p$, hence implies $p\vee  q$.
solution: Try $* = \wedge ,\ \square=\vee$: $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \to  (p \vee  q) \equiv  {\sim}(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  (p \vee  q)$.
$= ({\sim}p \vee  q) \vee  (p \vee  q)$.
$= ({\sim}p \vee  p) \vee  (q \vee  q) = \mathrm{t} \vee  q = \mathrm{t}$: a tautology.
Try $* = \wedge ,\ \square=\wedge$: at $p=T,\ q=F$, $p\wedge {\sim}q=T$ but $p\wedge  q=F$: false.
Try $* = \vee ,\ \square=\wedge$ and $* = \vee ,\ \square = \vee$: at $p=q=F$, $p\vee {\sim}q=T$ while $p\wedge  q=F$ and $p\vee  q=F$: false.
Only $(*,\square)=(\wedge ,\vee )$ works. Answer: (A).
questions.source_note: PDF checks only option (A); the other three combinations were added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Search for falsifying rows: premise true, conclusion false.
solution: With $*=\wedge$ the premise is true only at $p=T,\ q=F$; there $p\vee  q=T$ but $p\wedge  q=F$. So $\square$ must be $\vee$ (rules out (B)).
With $*=\vee$ the premise $p\vee {\sim}q$ is true at $p=q=F$, where both $p\wedge  q$ and $p\vee  q$ are false; so no $\square$ works (rules out (C), (D)).
Remaining: $*=\wedge ,\ \square=\vee$. Answer: (A).

useful_results: $(p \wedge  X) \to  (p \vee  Y)$ is a tautology for all $X,Y$: the premise forces $p$ true, hence the conclusion.
$p \wedge  {\sim}q$ is a stronger statement than $p \vee  q$, so $(p\wedge {\sim}q)\to (p\vee  q)$ always holds.
In 'which connective' problems, test a connective by hunting for a falsifying row.

questions.question: Negation of the statement $(p \vee  r) \to  (q \vee  r)$ is
questions.key_idea: ${\sim}(X\to  Y)=X\wedge {\sim}Y$; then ${\sim}(q\vee  r)={\sim}q\wedge {\sim}r$ and the factor $p\vee  r$ collapses.
solution: $(p \vee  r) \to  (q \vee  r) \equiv  {\sim}(p \vee  r) \vee  (q \vee  r)$.
Its negation is ${\sim}[{\sim}(p \vee  r) \vee  (q \vee  r)] = (p \vee  r) \wedge  {\sim}(q \vee  r)$.
${\sim}(q \vee  r) = {\sim}q \wedge  {\sim}r$, so this is $(p \vee  r) \wedge  ({\sim}q \wedge  {\sim}r)$.
Regroup: $[(p \vee  r) \wedge  {\sim}r] \wedge  {\sim}q$.
Distribute: $[(p \wedge  {\sim}r) \vee  (r \wedge  {\sim}r)] \wedge  {\sim}q = [(p \wedge  {\sim}r) \vee  \mathrm{c}] \wedge  {\sim}q$.
$= (p \wedge  {\sim}r) \wedge  {\sim}q = p \wedge  {\sim}q \wedge  {\sim}r$.
Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the only row where the conditional is false.
solution: $(p \vee  r) \to  (q \vee  r)$ is false iff $p \vee  r$ is true and $q \vee  r$ is false.
$q \vee  r$ false forces $q=F$ and $r=F$.
Then $p \vee  r = p$ must be true: $p=T$.
So the negation is true only for $(p,q,r)=(T,F,F)$, which is $p \wedge  {\sim}q \wedge  {\sim}r$. Answer: (D).

useful_results: ${\sim}(X \to  Y) \equiv  X \wedge  {\sim}Y$.
$(p \vee  r) \wedge  {\sim}r \equiv  p \wedge  {\sim}r$ (the factor $r$ is killed by ${\sim}r$).
A conjunction of literals describes exactly one assignment of its variables.

questions.question: Which of the following is equivalent to the Boolean expression $p \wedge  {\sim}q$?
questions.key_idea: ${\sim}(p\to  q)\equiv  p\wedge {\sim}q$.
solution: (A): $p \to  q \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q$, so ${\sim}(p \to  q) = {\sim}({\sim}p \vee  q) = p \wedge  {\sim}q$. Equivalent.
(B): ${\sim}(p \to  {\sim}q) = {\sim}({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q) = p \wedge  q$. Not equivalent.
(C): ${\sim}p \to  {\sim}q = {\sim}({\sim}p) \vee  {\sim}q = p \vee  {\sim}q$. Not equivalent.
(D): ${\sim}(q \to  p) = {\sim}({\sim}q \vee  p) = q \wedge  {\sim}p$. Not equivalent.
Answer: (A).
questions.correction_note: PDF's option (d) reads '~(q->p) => ~(~q v p) => q v ~p'; but ~(~q v p) = q ^ ~p (De Morgan), not q v ~p. The conclusion (D not equivalent) still holds.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use two test assignments: $p\wedge {\sim}q$ is true only at $p=T,\ q=F$.
solution: At $(p,q)=(T,F)$: $p\wedge {\sim}q=T$. (A) ${\sim}(T\to  F)=T$; (B) ${\sim}(T\to  T)=F$; (C) ${\sim}p\to {\sim}q=F\to  T=T$; (D) ${\sim}(F\to  T)=F$. This leaves (A) and (C).
At $(p,q)=(F,F)$: $p\wedge {\sim}q=F$. (C) ${\sim}p \to  {\sim}q = T \to  T = T$, so (C) is rejected.
(A) at $(F,F)$ is ${\sim}(F\to  F)=F$, as required. Answer: (A).

useful_results: ${\sim}(p \to  q) \equiv  p \wedge  {\sim}q$ and ${\sim}(q \to  p) \equiv  q \wedge  {\sim}p$.
${\sim}(p \to  {\sim}q) \equiv  p \wedge  q$ and ${\sim}p \to  {\sim}q \equiv  q \to  p$.
Two statements are equivalent iff they agree in every row: test them at the rows where the target is true or false.

questions.question: The number of choices for $\Delta \in \{\wedge ,\ \vee ,\ \to ,\ \leftrightarrow \}$, such that $(p\,\Delta\, q) \to  ((p\,\Delta\, {\sim}q) \vee  (({\sim}p)\,\Delta\, q))$ is a tautology, is
questions.key_idea: A conditional fails only when the premise is true and the conclusion false; test each of the four connectives for such a row.
solution: $\Delta=\wedge$: premise $p\wedge  q$ is true at $p=q=T$, while the conclusion $(p\wedge {\sim}q)\vee ({\sim}p\wedge  q)$ is $F\vee  F=F$. Fails.
$\Delta=\vee$: conclusion $(p\vee {\sim}q)\vee ({\sim}p\vee  q)$ contains $p\vee {\sim}p$, so it is always true. A tautology.
$\Delta=\to$: conclusion $(p\to {\sim}q)\vee ({\sim}p\to  q) = ({\sim}p\vee {\sim}q)\vee (p\vee  q)$ contains $p\vee {\sim}p$: always true. A tautology.

$\Delta=\leftrightarrow$: $p\leftrightarrow {\sim}q \equiv  {\sim}(p\leftrightarrow  q)$ and ${\sim}p\leftrightarrow  q \equiv  {\sim}(p\leftrightarrow  q)$, so the conclusion is ${\sim}(p\leftrightarrow  q)$.
Then the statement is $(p\leftrightarrow  q) \to  {\sim}(p\leftrightarrow  q)$, which is false when $p=q$ (for example $p=q=T$). Fails.
So exactly two choices, $\Delta=\vee$ and $\Delta=\to$, work.
Answer: (B) 2.
questions.source_note: PDF only states 'must be true when Delta = v & =>' without any working; the four-case check is written here.

alternate_solutions.idea: Think of the conclusion as 'the pair $(p,q)$ is not equal-valued in a certain sense' and count rows where each connective's premise holds.
solution: For every $\Delta$ the premise $p\Delta q$ and the two pieces $p\Delta{\sim}q$, ${\sim}p\Delta q$ can be read row by row. Rows: $(T,T),(T,F),(F,T),(F,F)$.
$\wedge$: premise true at $(T,T)$ only, conclusion pieces $p\wedge {\sim}q$ and ${\sim}p\wedge  q$ true only at $(T,F)$ and $(F,T)$: no overlap, fails.
$\leftrightarrow$: premise true at $(T,T)$ and $(F,F)$, conclusion pieces true at $(T,F)$ and $(F,T)$: no overlap, fails.

$\vee$: $p\vee {\sim}q$ fails only at $(F,T)$ and ${\sim}p\vee  q$ fails only at $(T,F)$, so the conclusion is true in every row. $\to$: $p\to {\sim}q$ fails only at $(T,T)$ and ${\sim}p\to  q$ fails only at $(F,F)$, again true in every row. Both conditionals never fail.
Hence 2. Answer: (B).

useful_results: Rows where $p\Delta{\sim}q$ or ${\sim}p\Delta q$ holds: for $\vee$ and $\to$ they cover all four rows; for $\wedge$ and $\leftrightarrow$ they cover exactly the rows with $p\ne q$.
$p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q \equiv  {\sim}p \leftrightarrow  q \equiv  {\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  q)$.
Counting 'how many connectives make a form a tautology' is done by testing each connective against its falsifier.

questions.question: Consider the following statements: $A$: Rishi is a judge. $B$: Rishi is honest. $C$: Rishi is not arrogant. The negation of the statement 'if Rishi is a judge and he is not arrogant, then he is honest' is:
questions.key_idea: Translate to $(A\wedge  C)\to  B$ and use ${\sim}(X\to  Y)=X\wedge {\sim}Y$.
solution: 'Judge and not arrogant' is $A \wedge  C$; the statement is $(A \wedge  C) \to  B$.
$(A \wedge  C) \to  B \equiv  {\sim}(A \wedge  C) \vee  B$.
Negation: ${\sim}[{\sim}(A \wedge  C) \vee  B] = (A \wedge  C) \wedge  {\sim}B$.
Reordering, $(A\wedge  C)\wedge {\sim}B = ({\sim}B) \wedge  (A \wedge  C)$.
Answer: (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: A conditional promise is broken exactly when its hypothesis holds and its conclusion fails; describe that situation.
solution: The claim 'judge and not arrogant implies honest' is refuted by a Rishi who is a judge, is not arrogant, and is not honest.
That is $A \wedge  C \wedge  {\sim}B$, i.e. $({\sim}B)\wedge (A\wedge  C)$: option (B).
(A), (C), (D) are conditionals; the negation of a conditional is never a conditional. Answer: (B).

useful_results: ${\sim}(X \to  Y) \equiv  X \wedge  {\sim}Y$: the negation of an implication is a conjunction, never an implication.
Translate 'not arrogant' as a statement ($C$) in its own right; do not negate it twice.
Options that are themselves conditionals can be rejected immediately.

questions.question: Consider the following two propositions: $P_1$: ${\sim}(p \to  {\sim}q)$ and $P_2$: $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \wedge  (({\sim}p) \vee  q)$. If the proposition $p \to  (({\sim}p) \vee  q)$ is evaluated as False then:
questions.key_idea: A false conditional means $p=T$ and ${\sim}p \vee  q$ false, which fixes $p=T,\ q=F$.
solution: $p \to  (({\sim}p) \vee  q)$ is False only if $p=T$ and $({\sim}p)\vee  q$ is False.
$({\sim}p) \vee  q$ false with $p=T$ means $q=F$. So $p=T,\ q=F$.
$P_1$: $p \to  {\sim}q = T \to  T = T$, so $P_1 = {\sim}(T) = F$.
$P_2$: $p \wedge  {\sim}q = T$ and $({\sim}p)\vee  q = F\vee  F = F$, so $P_2 = T \wedge  F = F$.
Both are false. Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Simplify the two propositions symbolically; both are fallacies-or-nearly, so their values do not even depend on the data.
solution: $P_1 = {\sim}(p \to  {\sim}q) = p \wedge  q$.
$P_2 = (p \wedge  {\sim}q) \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  q) = {\sim}(p \to  q) \wedge  (p \to  q) \equiv  \mathrm{c}$: always false.
The given condition gives $p=T,\ q=F$, so $P_1 = p\wedge  q = F$. $P_2$ is false regardless.
Both are false. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $p \to  ({\sim}p \vee  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q \equiv  p \to  q$, so the given proposition is false only at $(T,F)$.
${\sim}(p \to  {\sim}q) \equiv  p \wedge  q$.
$X \wedge  {\sim}X$ is always false: $P_2 = {\sim}(p\to  q) \wedge  (p\to  q)$.

questions.question: The negation of the Boolean expression $(({\sim}q) \wedge  p) \to  (({\sim}p) \vee  q)$ is logically equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: Simplify the expression first: it equals $p\to  q$, so its negation is ${\sim}(p\to  q)$.
solution: Negation: ${\sim}[(({\sim}q) \wedge  p) \to  (({\sim}p) \vee  q)]$.
Remove the conditional: $= {\sim}[{\sim}({\sim}q \wedge  p) \vee  ({\sim}p \vee  q)]$.
De Morgan inside: $= {\sim}[(q \vee  {\sim}p) \vee  ({\sim}p \vee  q)]$.
Combine the repeats: $= {\sim}({\sim}p \vee  q)$.
${\sim}p \vee  q = p \to  q$, so the negation is ${\sim}(p \to  q)$.
Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Observe that the premise ${\sim}q\wedge  p$ is exactly ${\sim}(p\to  q)$ and the conclusion ${\sim}p\vee  q$ is $p\to  q$.
solution: ${\sim}q \wedge  p \equiv  {\sim}({\sim}p \vee  q)$ and ${\sim}p \vee  q$ are exact negatives: with $X=p\to  q$ the expression is ${\sim}X \to  X$.
${\sim}X \to  X \equiv  X \vee  X \equiv  X$, so the expression is $p\to  q$.
Its negation is ${\sim}(p \to  q)$. Answer: (C).

useful_results: ${\sim}X \to  X \equiv  X$ ('if $X$ is false then $X$ is true' just says $X$).
$p \wedge  {\sim}q \equiv  {\sim}(p \to  q)$.
The expression $({\sim}q \wedge  p) \to  ({\sim}p \vee  q)$ is not a tautology: it is false at $p=T,\ q=F$.

questions.question:
Let $\Delta,
abla \in \{\wedge ,\ \vee \}$ be such that $p 
abla q 	o  ((p\,\Delta\, q)
abla r)$ is a tautology. Then $(p 
abla q)\,\Delta\, r$ is logically equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: Only $\Delta=\nabla=\vee$ gives a tautology; then $(p\vee  q)\vee  r$ is just a regrouping of $(p\vee  r)\vee  q$.
solution: Case I, $\Delta=\nabla=\wedge$: $(p\wedge  q) \to  ((p\wedge  q)\wedge  r)$ is false at $p=q=T,\ r=F$. Not a tautology.
Case II, $\Delta=\nabla=\vee$: $(p\vee  q) \to  ((p\vee  q)\vee  r)$ is a tautology ($X\to (X\vee  r)$).
Case III, $\Delta=\vee ,\ \nabla=\wedge$: $(p\wedge  q) \to  ((p\vee  q)\wedge  r)$ is false at $p=q=T,\ r=F$. Not a tautology.
Case IV, $\Delta=\wedge ,\ \nabla=\vee$: $(p\vee  q) \to  ((p\wedge  q)\vee  r)$ is false at $p=T,\ q=F,\ r=F$. Not a tautology.
So $\Delta=\nabla=\vee$.
Then $(p\nabla q)\Delta r = (p\vee  q)\vee  r$, which by regrouping equals $(p\vee  r)\vee  q$.
Answer: (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the shape of the tautology: the premise is $X$, the conclusion must contain $X$ as a part.
solution:
With $X = p
abla q$ the statement is $X 	o  (X' 
abla r)$ where $X'=p\Delta q$. For this to hold whenever $X$ is true, we need $X' 
abla r$ true whenever $p
abla q$ is true.
If $\nabla=\wedge$: $p\wedge  q$ true at $p=q=T$ and then $(p\Delta q)\wedge  r$ needs $r$ true: fails at $r=F$. So $\nabla=\vee$.
If $\nabla=\vee$ and $\Delta=\wedge$: at $p=T,q=F,r=F$ the premise $p\vee  q$ is true but $(p\wedge  q)\vee  r=F$. So $\Delta=\vee$.
Hence $\Delta=\nabla=\vee$ and $(p\vee  q)\vee  r \equiv  (p\vee  r)\vee  q$. Answer: (A).

useful_results: $X \to  (X \vee  r)$ is a tautology for all $X, r$ (addition); $X \to  (X \wedge  r)$ is not.
$\vee$ and $\wedge$ are associative and commutative, so $(p\vee  q)\vee  r \equiv  (p\vee  r)\vee  q \equiv  p\vee  (q\vee  r)$.
For connective-identification questions, eliminate options with a single falsifying row.

questions.question: Let $r \in \{p, q, {\sim}p, {\sim}q\}$ be such that the logical statement $r \vee  ({\sim}p) \to  (p \wedge  q) \vee  r$ is a tautology. Then $r$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Try $r={\sim}p$: the premise and the conclusion both reduce to ${\sim}p\,$ and ${\sim}p \vee  q$, and ${\sim}p \to  ({\sim}p\vee  q)$ is always true.
solution: Test $r={\sim}p$: premise $r\vee ({\sim}p) = {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}p = {\sim}p$.
Conclusion $(p\wedge  q)\vee  r = (p\wedge  q)\vee  {\sim}p = (p\vee  {\sim}p)\wedge (q\vee  {\sim}p) = \mathrm{t} \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  q) = {\sim}p \vee  q$.
So the statement is ${\sim}p \to  ({\sim}p \vee  q)$, which is a tautology ($X\to (X\vee  q)$).
Test $r=p$: premise $p\vee {\sim}p=\mathrm{t}$; conclusion $(p\wedge  q)\vee  p = p$. $\mathrm{t}\to  p = p$ is not a tautology.
Test $r=q$: premise $q\vee {\sim}p$; conclusion $(p\wedge  q)\vee  q = q$. $({\sim}p\vee  q)\to  q$ is false at $p=q=F$.
Test $r={\sim}q$: premise ${\sim}q\vee {\sim}p$; conclusion $(p\wedge  q)\vee  {\sim}q = p\vee  {\sim}q$. At $p=F,\ q=T$ the premise is true, the conclusion false.
Only $r={\sim}p$ works. Answer: (C).
questions.correction_note: PDF's working says '(p v q) v ~p = p' and concludes '~p => p = tautology'. Both are wrong: (p ^ q) v ~p equals ~p v q, and ~p => p is equivalent to p, not a tautology. The correct statement is ~p => (~p v q), a tautology. Answer C unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $p=T$ and $p=F$ to read off what $r$ must satisfy.
solution: At $p=F$ the premise is $r\vee {\sim}p=T$, so the conclusion $(p\wedge  q)\vee  r = r$ must be true: $r$ must be T when $p=F$.
Among $p,q,{\sim}p,{\sim}q$: $p$ is F at $p=F$, so $r=p$ fails; $q$ and ${\sim}q$ can be F when $p=F$ (take $q=F$ for $r=q$, $q=T$ for $r={\sim}q$), so they fail.
$r={\sim}p$ is T whenever $p=F$ and, at $p=T$, the conclusion is $q\vee  r$, no constraint is broken because the premise $r\vee {\sim}p = F$.
So $r={\sim}p$. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $X \to  (X \vee  Y)$ is a tautology (addition).
$(p \wedge  q) \vee  {\sim}p \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q$ (since $p \vee  {\sim}p$ is true).
When an unknown statement must make an implication true, look at the rows where the premise holds and see what the conclusion forces on the unknown.

questions.question: The Boolean expression $({\sim}(p \wedge  q)) \vee  q$ is equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: The expression is a tautology, so the equivalent option is the tautologous one.
solution: ${\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  q = ({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q) \vee  q$.
Regroup: $= {\sim}p \vee  ({\sim}q \vee  q)$.
${\sim}q \vee  q = \mathrm{t}$, so this is ${\sim}p \vee  \mathrm{t}$.
${\sim}p \vee  \mathrm{t} = \mathrm{t}$: the expression is a tautology.
(D): $p \to  (p \vee  q)$ is ${\sim}p \vee  p \vee  q = \mathrm{t}$: a tautology (see the truth table: T, T, T, T).
(A) $q \to  (p \wedge  q) = {\sim}q \vee  p$, (B) $p \to  q = {\sim}p \vee  q$, (C) $p \to  (p \to  q) = {\sim}p \vee  q$ are not tautologies.
Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: A disjunction with $q$ and ${\sim}(p\wedge  q)$: if $q$ is false the second term is true.
solution: If $q=T$ the expression is true because of the term $q$.
If $q=F$ then $p\wedge  q=F$, so ${\sim}(p\wedge  q)=T$ and the expression is true.
So it is true in all cases, a tautology. The only tautologous option is (D), since $p\to (p\vee  q)$ is true whenever $p$ is.
Answer: (D).

useful_results: ${\sim}(X \wedge  Y) \vee  Y \equiv  {\sim}X \vee  {\sim}Y \vee  Y \equiv  \mathrm{t}$: a statement $Y$ and the negation of $X\wedge  Y$ cover all cases.
$p \to  (p \vee  q)$ is a tautology (addition).
If the expression is a tautology, 'equivalent to' means 'also a tautology'.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is a tautology?
questions.key_idea: $X\wedge {\sim}X$ is a fallacy and $X\vee {\sim}X$ is a tautology; spot which options contain which.
solution: (A): $({\sim}q \wedge  p) \wedge  q = ({\sim}q \wedge  q) \wedge  p = \mathrm{c} \wedge  p = \mathrm{c}$. Not a tautology.
(B): $({\sim}q \wedge  p) \wedge  (p \wedge  {\sim}p) = ({\sim}q \wedge  p) \wedge  \mathrm{c} = \mathrm{c}$. Not a tautology.
(C): $({\sim}q \wedge  p) \vee  (p \vee  {\sim}p) = ({\sim}q \wedge  p) \vee  \mathrm{t} = \mathrm{t}$. A tautology.
(D): $(p \wedge  q) \wedge  {\sim}(p \wedge  q)$ has the form $X \wedge  {\sim}X = \mathrm{c}$. Not a tautology.
Answer: (C).
questions.correction_note: PDF's check of option (D) expands ~(p^q) as '~p ^ ~q' (it is ~p v ~q); the final value F is the same because X ^ ~X is false, so shown here with X = p ^ q.

alternate_solutions.idea: Label each option by its outer connective and the complementary pair it contains.
solution: (A), (B), (D) are conjunctions, so each is true only if every conjunct is true. (A) needs ${\sim}q$ and $q$ together; (B) needs $p$ and ${\sim}p$; (D) needs $X$ and ${\sim}X$. All impossible.
(C) is a disjunction one of whose parts, $p\vee {\sim}p$, is always true, so it is always true.
Answer: (C).

useful_results: A conjunction containing both $X$ and ${\sim}X$ is a fallacy; a disjunction containing both is a tautology.
${\sim}(p \wedge  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q$ (not ${\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q$).
Check options by looking for complementary pairs before any table.

questions.question: Let $p,q,r$ be three logical statements. Consider the compound statements $S_1: (({\sim}p) \vee  q) \vee  (({\sim}p) \vee  r)$ and $S_2: p \to  (q \vee  r)$. Then, which of the following is NOT true?
options: If $S_2$ is True, then $S_1$ is True
If $S_2$ is False, then $S_1$ is False
If $S_2$ is False, then $S_1$ is True
If $S_1$ is False, then $S_2$ is False
questions.key_idea: $S_1$ and $S_2$ are logically equivalent, so they always have the same truth value.
solution: $S_2 = p \to  (q \vee  r) \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  (q \vee  r)$.
$S_1 = ({\sim}p \vee  q) \vee  ({\sim}p \vee  r) = {\sim}p \vee  q \vee  r$ (the repeated ${\sim}p$ merges).
So $S_1$ and $S_2$ are the same statement: $S_1 \equiv  S_2$.
Equivalent statements always have equal truth values. Hence (A) is true, (B) is true, (D) is true.
(C) says that when $S_2$ is False then $S_1$ is True; but $S_1$ is then also False. So (C) is NOT true.
Answer: (C).
questions.correction_note: PDF labels the statement p -> (q v r) as 'S1' and then shows it equals S1; it is S2 (the line 'S1: p->(q v r)' should read 'S2'). Meaning and answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the single row where each statement is false and compare.
solution: $S_2$ is false iff $p=T$ and $q \vee  r$ is false: $(p,q,r)=(T,F,F)$ only.
$S_1 = {\sim}p \vee  q \vee  r$ is a disjunction, so it is false iff all three disjuncts are false: $p=T,\ q=F,\ r=F$ only.
Same single row, so the two statements always agree.
Therefore 'If $S_2$ is False then $S_1$ is True' cannot hold. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $p \to  (q \vee  r) \equiv  (p \to  q) \vee  (p \to  r) \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q \vee  r$.
A disjunction of $n$ distinct literals is false in exactly one assignment of those $n$ variables.
If two statements are equivalent, 'if one is true then the other is true' and 'if one is false then the other is false' both hold.

questions.question: Let $\Delta \in \{\wedge ,\ \vee ,\ \to ,\ \leftrightarrow \}$ be such that $(p \wedge  q)\,\Delta\,((p \vee  q) \to  q)$ is a tautology. Then $\Delta$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: If $p\wedge  q$ is true then $q$ is true, so $(p\vee  q)\to  q$ is true: $(p\wedge  q)\to ((p\vee  q)\to  q)$ cannot fail.
solution: Rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF: $p\wedge  q$ = T, F, F, F and $p\vee  q$ = T, T, T, F.
$(p \vee  q) \to  q$ = T, F, T, T.
$\Delta=\to$: $(p\wedge  q) \to  ((p\vee  q)\to  q)$ = T, T, T, T. A tautology.
$\Delta=\wedge$: $(p\wedge  q)\wedge ((p\vee  q)\to  q)$ = T, F, F, F. Not a tautology.
$\Delta=\vee$: $(p\wedge  q)\vee ((p\vee  q)\to  q)$ = T, F, T, T. Not a tautology (row TF).
$\Delta=\leftrightarrow$: $(p\wedge  q)\leftrightarrow ((p\vee  q)\to  q)$ = T, T, F, F. Not a tautology.
So $\Delta$ is $\to$. Answer: (C).
questions.source_note: PDF shows only the table for the correct connective; the other three were added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Argue with the single row where the premise $p\wedge  q$ is true.
solution: For $\Delta=\to$: the conditional fails only if $p\wedge  q$ is true and $(p\vee  q)\to  q$ false. But $p\wedge  q$ true means $q=T$, making $(p\vee  q)\to  q$ true. So it never fails.
For $\Delta=\wedge ,\vee ,\leftrightarrow$ look at the row $p=F,\ q=T$: $p\wedge  q=F$ and $(p\vee  q)\to  q = T\to  T=T$. Then $\wedge$ gives F; $\leftrightarrow$ gives F.
For $\Delta=\vee$ look at $p=T,\ q=F$: $p\wedge  q=F$ and $(p\vee  q)\to  q=T\to  F=F$, giving F. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $(p \wedge  q) \to  X$ is a tautology whenever $q$ (or $p$) already forces $X$ true.
$(p \vee  q) \to  q \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q \equiv  p \to  q$.
So the expression is $(p \wedge  q) \to  (p \to  q)$, the same as Q23(C).

questions.question: Negation of the boolean statement $(p \vee  q) \to  (({\sim}r) \vee  p)$ is equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: ${\sim}(X\to  Y)=X\wedge {\sim}Y$: here $(p\vee  q)\wedge  r\wedge  {\sim}p$, and $(p\vee  q)\wedge {\sim}p$ collapses to $q\wedge {\sim}p$.
solution: $(p \vee  q) \to  (({\sim}r) \vee  p) \equiv  {\sim}(p \vee  q) \vee  ({\sim}r \vee  p)$.
De Morgan: $= ({\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  (p \vee  {\sim}r)$.
Distribute ${\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q$ over the $p$: $[({\sim}p \vee  p) \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  p)] \vee  {\sim}r$.
$= (\mathrm{t} \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  p)) \vee  {\sim}r = (p \vee  {\sim}q) \vee  {\sim}r$.
Negation: ${\sim}[({\sim}q \vee  p) \vee  {\sim}r] = q \wedge  {\sim}p \wedge  r$.
$= ({\sim}p) \wedge  q \wedge  r$. Answer: (C).
questions.correction_note: PDF's third line prints (~p v q) v (p v ~r); the De Morgan result is (~p ^ ~q) v (p v ~r). Corrected; the PDF also stops before simplifying the final negation, which is completed here.

alternate_solutions.idea: The conditional is false in exactly one way; solve for it.
solution: $(p\vee  q)\to ({\sim}r\vee  p)$ is false iff $p\vee  q$ is true and ${\sim}r\vee  p$ is false.
${\sim}r \vee  p$ false means $r=T$ and $p=F$.
Then $p\vee  q = q$ must be true: $q=T$.
So the negation is true only for $(p,q,r)=(F,T,T)$, i.e. ${\sim}p \wedge  q \wedge  r$. Answer: (C).

useful_results: ${\sim}(X \to  Y) \equiv  X \wedge  {\sim}Y$; a conjunction of literals pins down one row, so the answer can be read off that row.
$(p \vee  q) \wedge  {\sim}p \equiv  {\sim}p \wedge  q$.
$X \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y) \equiv  X \vee  Y$ (used in the main solution with $X=p$).

questions.question: The maximum number of compound propositions, out of $p \vee  r \vee  s,\ p \vee  r \vee  {\sim}s,\ p \vee  {\sim}q \vee  s,\ {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}r \vee  s,\ {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}r \vee  {\sim}s,\ {\sim}p \vee  q \vee  {\sim}s,\ q \vee  r \vee  {\sim}s,\ q \vee  {\sim}r \vee  {\sim}s,\ {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q \vee  {\sim}s$ that can be made simultaneously true by an assignment of the truth values to $p,\ q,\ r$ and $s$, is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Setting $s=F$ makes all six propositions containing ${\sim}s$ true; the other three then only need $p\vee  r$, $p\vee {\sim}q$, ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}r$.
solution: There are 9 propositions, each a disjunction of three literals.

Six of them contain ${\sim}s$: $p\vee  r\vee {\sim}s$, ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}r\vee {\sim}s$, ${\sim}p\vee  q\vee {\sim}s$, $q\vee  r\vee {\sim}s$, $q\vee {\sim}r\vee {\sim}s$, ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}q\vee {\sim}s$.
Take $s=F$. Then ${\sim}s=T$, so these six are all true whatever $p,q,r$ are.
The other three, $p\vee  r\vee  s$, $p\vee {\sim}q\vee  s$, ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}r\vee  s$, become $p\vee  r$, $p\vee {\sim}q$ and ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}r$.
Choose $p=T,\ r=F$ (and any $q$): $p\vee  r=T$, $p\vee {\sim}q=T$ and ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}r=F\vee  T=T$.
So all nine propositions are true at, e.g., $(p,q,r,s)=(T,T,F,F)$.
The maximum cannot exceed the total 9, so it is 9. Answer: 9.
questions.source_note: PDF's solution is two lines ('s false makes 6 true; the remaining 3 with P->T, r->F'); written out in full.

alternate_solutions.idea: Try the other value $s=T$: the clauses without ${\sim}s$ become 2-literal conditions that can be solved directly.
solution: Take $s=T$. The three propositions containing $s$ are true; the other six become $p\vee  r$, ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}r$, ${\sim}p\vee  q$, $q\vee  r$, $q\vee {\sim}r$, ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}q$.
${\sim}p\vee  q$ and ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}q$ both true force $p=F$ (if $p=T$ we would need $q$ and ${\sim}q$).
With $p=F$: $p\vee  r$ forces $r=T$; then $q\vee {\sim}r$ forces $q=T$.
Check $(p,q,r,s)=(F,T,T,T)$: ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}r=T$, ${\sim}p\vee  q=T$, $q\vee  r=T$, $q\vee {\sim}r=T$, ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}q=T$, $p\vee  r=T$. All six true, so all nine are true again.
So 9 propositions are simultaneously true by a second, independent assignment. Answer: 9.

useful_results: A set of disjunctions (clauses) is simultaneously satisfiable iff some assignment makes every clause true; fixing one variable to satisfy many clauses at once is the standard first move.
A clause containing a literal is satisfied outright once that literal is made true.
Here the four variables give 16 assignments; exactly 4 of them satisfy all nine clauses (checked by listing).

questions.question: Which of the following statements is a tautology?
questions.key_idea: $q\to (X\vee  q)$ is the 'addition' rule: if $q$ is true then any disjunction containing $q$ is true.
solution: Truth table, rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF: ${\sim}p \vee  q$ = T, F, T, T.
(A) $({\sim}p \vee  q) \to  p$ = T, T, F, F: not a tautology.
(B) $p \to  ({\sim}p \vee  q)$ = T, F, T, T: not a tautology.
(C) $({\sim}p \vee  q) \to  q$ = T, T, T, F: not a tautology.
(D) $q \to  ({\sim}p \vee  q)$ = T, T, T, T: a tautology.
Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Argue with the premise: $q$ true makes ${\sim}p\vee  q$ true, so (D) cannot fail; find a failing row for each other option.
solution: (D) fails only if $q=T$ and ${\sim}p\vee  q=F$, but $q=T$ makes the disjunction true. So (D) never fails.
(A) fails at $p=F,\ q=T$ (${\sim}p\vee  q=T$, $p=F$). (B) fails at $p=T,\ q=F$ ($p=T$, ${\sim}p\vee  q=F$). (C) fails at $p=q=F$ (${\sim}p\vee  q=T$, $q=F$).
Answer: (D).

useful_results: Addition: $X \to  (X \vee  Y)$ and $Y \to  (X \vee  Y)$ are tautologies.
$p \to  ({\sim}p \vee  q) \equiv  p \to  (p \to  q)$, which is ${\sim}p \vee  q$, not a tautology.
An implication is a tautology iff its premise implies its conclusion in every row.

questions.question: Consider the following statements: $P$: Ramu is intelligent. $Q$: Ramu is rich. $R$: Ramu is not honest. The negation of the statement 'Ramu is intelligent and honest if and only if Ramu is not rich' can be expressed as:
questions.key_idea: 'Honest' is ${\sim}R$, so the statement is $(P\wedge {\sim}R)\leftrightarrow {\sim}Q$; negating one side of $\leftrightarrow$ gives $(P\wedge {\sim}R)\leftrightarrow  Q$, i.e. both true or both false.
solution: 'Intelligent and honest' is $P \wedge  {\sim}R$ (honest $={\sim}R$); 'not rich' is ${\sim}Q$.
The statement is $(P \wedge  {\sim}R) \leftrightarrow  {\sim}Q$.
Negation: ${\sim}[(P \wedge  {\sim}R) \leftrightarrow  {\sim}Q]$.
Use $X\leftrightarrow  Y \equiv  ({\sim}X \vee  Y) \wedge  (X \vee  {\sim}Y)$: ${\sim}[(X\leftrightarrow  Y)] = (X \wedge  {\sim}Y) \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y)$.
With $X=P\wedge {\sim}R$ and $Y={\sim}Q$: $= ((P \wedge  {\sim}R) \wedge  Q) \vee  ({\sim}(P \wedge  {\sim}R) \wedge  {\sim}Q)$.
${\sim}(P \wedge  {\sim}R) = {\sim}P \vee  R$, so $= ((P \wedge  {\sim}R) \wedge  Q) \vee  (({\sim}Q) \wedge  (({\sim}P) \vee  R))$.
This is option (D). Answer: (D).
questions.source_note: PDF's first line has the first two tokens of the expansion in an intermediate form; steps rewritten cleanly (same result).

alternate_solutions.idea: Evaluate the statement at one convenient assignment and eliminate options.
solution: Take $(P,Q,R)=(T,T,F)$: $P\wedge {\sim}R=T$, ${\sim}Q=F$, so the statement is $T\leftrightarrow  F=F$ and its negation is True.
(A) contains the factor $(({\sim}Q)\wedge \dots)$ with ${\sim}Q=F$ in a conjunction: False. (B) first part $(P\wedge  R)\wedge  Q=F$, second part ${\sim}Q=F$: False. (C) False similarly.
(D): $((P\wedge {\sim}R)\wedge  Q) = T$, so the disjunction is True. Only (D) matches. Answer: (D).

useful_results: ${\sim}(X \leftrightarrow  Y) \equiv  (X \wedge  {\sim}Y) \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y) \equiv  X \leftrightarrow  {\sim}Y$.
Here $R$ is itself the negative statement 'Ramu is not honest', so 'honest' is ${\sim}R$; read each definition before translating.
A single well-chosen assignment can eliminate all but one option.

questions.question: The statement $({\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q)) \wedge  q$ is:
questions.key_idea: ${\sim}(p\leftrightarrow {\sim}q)=p\leftrightarrow  q$, and $(p\leftrightarrow  q)\wedge  q$ reduces to $p\wedge  q$, which is also $(p\to  q)\wedge  p$.
solution: ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q) \equiv  p \leftrightarrow  q$, so the statement is $(p \leftrightarrow  q) \wedge  q$.
Truth table, rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF: $p\leftrightarrow  q$ = T, F, F, T.
$(p \leftrightarrow  q) \wedge  q$ = T, F, F, F.
$(p \to  q) \wedge  q$ = T, F, T, F (differs in row FT): not equivalent, so (C) is false.
$(p \to  q) \wedge  p$ = T, F, F, F: identical to the given column, so (D) is true.
The column has both T and F, so (A) and (B) are false.
Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute the known value of $q$ into the biconditional and the conditional.
solution: In $(p\leftrightarrow  q)\wedge  q$ the factor $q$ must be true, and then $p\leftrightarrow  q$ becomes $p\leftrightarrow  T = p$. So the statement is $p\wedge  q$.
In $(p\to  q)\wedge  p$ the factor $p$ must be true, and then $p\to  q$ becomes $T\to  q = q$. So this is $p\wedge  q$ too.
They agree; $(p\to  q)\wedge  q$ equals $q$ instead. Answer: (D).

useful_results: ${\sim}(p \leftrightarrow  {\sim}q) \equiv  p \leftrightarrow  q$.
$(X \leftrightarrow  Y) \wedge  Y \equiv  X \wedge  Y$ and $(X \to  Y) \wedge  X \equiv  X \wedge  Y$ (modus-ponens flavour).
Inside a conjunction, each factor may be assumed true when simplifying the others.

questions.question: Negation of the Boolean expression $p \leftrightarrow  (q \to  p)$ is:
questions.key_idea: ${\sim}(X\leftrightarrow  Y)=(X\wedge {\sim}Y)\vee ({\sim}X\wedge  Y)$; one of the two pieces is a contradiction.
solution: ${\sim}(X \leftrightarrow  Y) \equiv  (X \wedge  {\sim}Y) \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y)$ with $X=p,\ Y=q\to  p$.
$p \wedge  {\sim}(q \to  p) = p \wedge  (q \wedge  {\sim}p) = (p \wedge  {\sim}p) \wedge  q = \mathrm{c}$.
$(q \to  p) \wedge  {\sim}p = ({\sim}q \vee  p) \wedge  {\sim}p = ({\sim}q \wedge  {\sim}p) \vee  (p \wedge  {\sim}p) = {\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q$.
Negation $= \mathrm{c} \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q) = {\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q$.
Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Split on the value of $p$.
solution: If $p=T$ then $q\to  p$ is true, so $p\leftrightarrow (q\to  p)=T\leftrightarrow  T=T$.
If $p=F$ then $q\to  p={\sim}q$, so $p\leftrightarrow (q\to  p)=F\leftrightarrow {\sim}q$, which is true iff ${\sim}q=F$, i.e. $q=T$.
So the expression is false only for $p=F,\ q=F$; its negation is true only there: ${\sim}p\wedge {\sim}q$. Answer: (D).

useful_results: $p \leftrightarrow  (q \to  p) \equiv  p \vee  q$: the biconditional is true iff $p$ or $q$ holds; so its negation is ${\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q$.
${\sim}(X \leftrightarrow  Y) \equiv  (X \wedge  {\sim}Y) \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y)$.
Case splitting on one variable is often the quickest way to evaluate a biconditional.

questions.question: $(p \wedge  r) \leftrightarrow  (p \wedge  ({\sim}q))$ is equivalent to $({\sim}p)$ when $r$ is:
questions.key_idea: If $p=F$ both sides are false and the biconditional is true; for $p=T$ the biconditional becomes $r\leftrightarrow {\sim}q$, which must be false for all $q$.
solution: Try $r=q$: $(p\wedge  q)\leftrightarrow (p\wedge {\sim}q)$.
Rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF: $p\wedge  q$ = T, F, F, F and $p\wedge {\sim}q$ = F, T, F, F.
The biconditional is F, F, T, T.
${\sim}p$ = F, F, T, T: equal.

Other choices: $r=p$ gives $p\leftrightarrow (p\wedge {\sim}q)$ = F, T, T, T (not ${\sim}p$); $r={\sim}q$ gives $(p\wedge {\sim}q)\leftrightarrow (p\wedge {\sim}q)$, a tautology; $r={\sim}p$ gives $\mathrm{c}\leftrightarrow (p\wedge {\sim}q)={\sim}(p\wedge {\sim}q)$ (not ${\sim}p$).
Only $r=q$ works. Answer: (C).
questions.source_note: PDF tries only r = q; the other three candidates were checked and added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split on $p$ and see what $r$ must do.
solution: If $p=F$: both $p\wedge  r$ and $p\wedge {\sim}q$ are false, so the biconditional is true; and ${\sim}p=T$. Consistent for every $r$.
If $p=T$: the biconditional is $r\leftrightarrow {\sim}q$ and must equal ${\sim}p=F$ for every $q$. So $r$ and ${\sim}q$ must always differ: $r=q$.
Check: $r\leftrightarrow {\sim}q$ with $r=q$ is $q\leftrightarrow {\sim}q=F$. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $X \leftrightarrow  {\sim}X \equiv  \mathrm{c}$ and $X \leftrightarrow  X \equiv  \mathrm{t}$: a biconditional between a statement and its negation is false.
$p \wedge  r$ with $p=T$ reduces to $r$: conjunction with a true factor disappears.
To find an unknown statement $r$, split on the other variables and solve the resulting condition.

questions.question: If the truth value of the statement $(P \wedge  ({\sim}R)) \to  (({\sim}R) \wedge  Q)$ is F, then the truth value of which of the following is F?
questions.key_idea: A false conditional pins down $P=T,\ R=F$ and then $Q=F$; evaluate the four options at that single row.
solution: $X \to  Y$ is false only when $X$ is true and $Y$ is false.
$X = P \wedge  {\sim}R$ true gives $P=T$ and $R=F$.
$Y = {\sim}R \wedge  Q$ with ${\sim}R=T$ is false only if $Q=F$.
So $(P,Q,R)=(T,F,F)$.
(A) $P\vee  Q \to  {\sim}R$: $T \to  T = T$.
(B) $R\vee  Q \to  {\sim}P$: $F \to  F = T$.
(C) ${\sim}(P\vee  Q) \to  {\sim}R$: $F \to  T = T$.
(D) ${\sim}(R\vee  Q) \to  {\sim}P$: $T \to  F = F$.
Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: For each option find its own single falsifying row and compare it with $(T,F,F)$.
solution: (A) is false iff $P\vee  Q$ is true and ${\sim}R$ false, so $R=T$: it cannot be false at $R=F$.
(B) is false iff $R\vee  Q$ true and ${\sim}P$ false ($P=T$): at $(T,F,F)$ we have $R\vee  Q=F$, so it is true.
(C) is false iff $P\vee  Q$ false (so $P=F$): not our row.
(D) is false iff $R\vee  Q$ false and ${\sim}P$ false: $R=Q=F,\ P=T$: exactly $(T,F,F)$. Answer: (D).

useful_results: A conditional has exactly one falsifying row condition: premise true, conclusion false.
Given that a compound statement is false, extract the truth values of the variables first, then evaluate.
${\sim}(R \vee  Q) \to  {\sim}P \equiv  (R \vee  Q) \vee  {\sim}P$ is false only when $R=Q=F,\ P=T$.

questions.question: Let the operations $*,\ \odot \in \{\wedge ,\ \vee \}$. If $(p * q) \odot (p \odot {\sim}q)$ is a tautology, then the ordered pair $(*,\ \odot)$ is:
questions.key_idea: With $\odot=\vee$ the expression contains $q\vee {\sim}q$; with $\odot=\wedge$ it contains $p$ as a conjunct and is false at $p=F$.
solution: Option (A), $*=\vee ,\ \odot=\wedge$: $(p\vee  q)\wedge (p\wedge {\sim}q) = p\wedge {\sim}q$ (the factor $p\wedge {\sim}q$ implies $p\vee  q$). Not a tautology.
Option (B), $*=\vee ,\ \odot=\vee$: $(p\vee  q)\vee (p\vee {\sim}q) = p\vee (q\vee {\sim}q) = p\vee \mathrm{t} = \mathrm{t}$. A tautology.
Option (C), $*=\wedge ,\ \odot=\wedge$: $(p\wedge  q)\wedge (p\wedge {\sim}q) = p\wedge (q\wedge {\sim}q) = \mathrm{c}$. Not a tautology.
Option (D), $*=\wedge ,\ \odot=\vee$: $(p\wedge  q)\vee (p\vee {\sim}q) = p\vee {\sim}q$ (since $p\wedge  q$ implies $p$). False at $p=F,\ q=T$. Not a tautology.
Only (B) works. Answer: (B).
questions.correction_note: PDF's check of option (A) writes (p v q) ^ (p v ~q) = p; with the operations of option (A) the second bracket is p ^ ~q (since the second operation is also AND), giving p ^ ~q. Neither is a tautology so the conclusion stands. PDF proves (B) by a Venn diagram; algebraic proof given.

alternate_solutions.idea: Search for falsifying rows by the shape of the outer connective.
solution: If $\odot=\wedge$, the expression has the conjunct $p\wedge {\sim}q$, which is false whenever $p=F$: never a tautology (rules out (A), (C)).
If $\odot=\vee$ the expression is $(p*q)\vee (p\vee {\sim}q)$. The second part is false only at $p=F,\ q=T$.
At that row $p*q = F*T$: with $*=\vee$ it is T (so the whole is true), with $*=\wedge$ it is F (the whole is false).
So $(\vee ,\vee )$ is a tautology and $(\wedge ,\vee )$ is not. Answer: (B).

useful_results: A conjunction is a tautology only if every conjunct is; a conjunction containing a non-tautology like $p\wedge {\sim}q$ is never one.
$(p \vee  q) \vee  (p \vee  {\sim}q) \equiv  p \vee  (q \vee  {\sim}q) \equiv  \mathrm{t}$.
$X \wedge  Y$ is a tautology only if both $X$ and $Y$ are; $X \vee  Y$ is a tautology as soon as one of them is.

questions.question: Let $p$: Ramesh listens to music. $q$: Ramesh is out of his village. $r$: It is Sunday. $s$: It is Saturday. Then the statement 'Ramesh listens to music only if he is in his village and it is Sunday or Saturday' can be expressed as:
questions.key_idea: '$A$ only if $B$' means $A\to  B$; 'in his village' is ${\sim}q$ and 'Sunday or Saturday' is $r\vee  s$.
solution: $p$: Ramesh listens to music; ${\sim}q$: he is in his village; $r\vee  s$: Sunday or Saturday.
'in his village and it is Sunday or Saturday' is $({\sim}q) \wedge  (r \vee  s)$.
'$A$ only if $B$' is $A \to  B$, with $A=p$.
So the statement is $p \to  (({\sim}q) \wedge  (r \vee  s))$.
Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the options at one assignment where the promise is clearly broken.
solution: Take $p=T$ (he listens), $q=T$ (he is out of his village), $r=T$: the promise is broken, so the statement is False.
(A) $({\sim}q\wedge (r\vee  s))\to  p = F\to  T = T$. (B) $(q\wedge (r\vee  s))\to  p = T\to  T = T$. (C) $p\to (q\wedge (r\vee  s)) = T\to  T = T$.
(D) $p\to ({\sim}q\wedge (r\vee  s)) = T\to  F = F$: the only option that is False. Answer: (D).

useful_results: '$A$ only if $B$' $=A\to  B$; '$A$ if $B$' $=B\to  A$; '$A$ if and only if $B$' $=A\leftrightarrow  B$.
'in the village' is the negation of 'out of the village', i.e. ${\sim}q$, so read the defined statements before translating.
'Sunday or Saturday' is a plain (inclusive) disjunction $r\vee  s$.

questions.question: The statement $(p \wedge  q) \to  (p \wedge  r)$ is equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: $X\to (p\wedge  r)$ with $X=p\wedge  q$ already containing $p$: the repeated $p$ is redundant.
solution: $(p \wedge  q) \to  (p \wedge  r) \equiv  {\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  (p \wedge  r) \equiv  ({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q) \vee  (p \wedge  r)$.
Regroup: $({\sim}p \vee  (p \wedge  r)) \vee  {\sim}q$.
Distribute: $({\sim}p \vee  p) \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  r) \vee  {\sim}q = (\mathrm{t} \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  r)) \vee  {\sim}q$.
$= ({\sim}p \vee  r) \vee  {\sim}q = ({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q) \vee  r$.
$= {\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  r$.
${\sim}(p\wedge  q) \vee  r \equiv  (p \wedge  q) \to  r$. Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Both sides are conditionals; compare their falsifying rows.
solution: $(p\wedge  q)\to (p\wedge  r)$ is false iff $p=q=T$ and $p\wedge  r$ false, i.e. $r=F$: only $(T,T,F)$.
(D) $(p\wedge  q)\to  r$ is false iff $p=q=T$ and $r=F$: the same single row.

(A) is false at $q=T,\ p=F$; (B) is false at $p=T,\ r=F$ with $q$ arbitrary, e.g. $(T,F,F)$, where the given statement is true; (C) is false at $p=r=T,\ q=F$, where the given statement is true. Answer: (D).

useful_results: $X \to  (X \wedge  Y) \equiv  X \to  Y$ and, with $X$ containing $p$: $(p\wedge  q) \to  (p \wedge  r) \equiv  (p \wedge  q) \to  r$.
Under the premise, any statement already implied by it can be added to or dropped from the conclusion.
Compare conditionals by their falsifying rows.

questions.question: The statement $(p \to  q) \vee  (p \to  r)$ is NOT equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: $(p\to  q)\vee (p\to  r) \equiv  {\sim}p\vee  q\vee  r$, false only at $(T,F,F)$; check which option is not false exactly there.
solution: $(p\to  q)\vee (p\to  r) = ({\sim}p\vee  q)\vee ({\sim}p\vee  r) = {\sim}p \vee  (q \vee  r)$.
So the statement is $p \to  (q \vee  r)$, which is option (C): equivalent.
(A): $(p\wedge {\sim}r)\to  q = {\sim}(p\wedge {\sim}r)\vee  q = ({\sim}p\vee  r)\vee  q = {\sim}p\vee  q\vee  r$: equivalent.
(D): $(p\wedge {\sim}q)\to  r = ({\sim}p\vee  q)\vee  r = {\sim}p\vee  q\vee  r$: equivalent.

(B): $({\sim}q)\to (({\sim}r)\vee  p) = q \vee  {\sim}r \vee  p$, which is $p\vee  q\vee {\sim}r$, not ${\sim}p\vee  q\vee  r$. Not equivalent (they differ at $p=T,\ q=F,\ r=F$: the first is false, (B) is true).
Answer: (B).
questions.source_note: PDF numbers the options (1),(3),(4) and never evaluates (B); the evaluation of (B) is added.

alternate_solutions.idea: The given statement is false only at one row; test the four options at that row.
solution: ${\sim}p\vee  q\vee  r$ is false only for $p=T,\ q=F,\ r=F$.
At $(T,F,F)$: (A) $(T\wedge  T)\to  F = F$; (C) $T\to  F=F$; (D) $(T\wedge  T)\to  F = F$.
(B): ${\sim}q=T$ and ${\sim}r\vee  p=T$, so (B) is $T\to  T=T$, not False: (B) is not equivalent.
