useful_results: $(p \to  q) \vee  (p \to  r) \equiv  p \to  (q \vee  r)$ and $(p \to  q) \wedge  (p \to  r) \equiv  p \to  (q \wedge  r)$.
$(p \wedge  {\sim}r) \to  q \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  r \vee  q$ and $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \to  r \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q \vee  r$: moving a negated literal to the other side of a conditional.
A disjunction of three literals is false in exactly one row; two such statements are equivalent iff they use the same literals.

questions.question: The compound statement $({\sim}(P \wedge  Q)) \vee  (({\sim}P) \wedge  Q) \to  (({\sim}P) \wedge  ({\sim}Q))$ is equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: The premise ${\sim}(P\wedge  Q)\vee ({\sim}P\wedge  Q)$ is just ${\sim}(P\wedge  Q)$, so the statement is ${\sim}(P\wedge  Q)\to ({\sim}P\wedge {\sim}Q)$, which says $P\leftrightarrow  Q$.
solution: Let $r={\sim}(P\wedge  Q)\vee ({\sim}P\wedge  Q)$ and $s={\sim}P\wedge {\sim}Q$; the statement is $r \to  s$.
Truth table, rows $(P,Q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF: ${\sim}(P\wedge  Q)$ = F, T, T, T and $({\sim}P)\wedge  Q$ = F, F, T, F.
$r$ = F, T, T, T and $s$ = F, F, F, T.
$r \to  s$ = T, F, F, T.
This column is the truth table of $P\leftrightarrow  Q$ (true exactly when $P$ and $Q$ agree).
Option (D): $(({\sim}P)\vee  Q)\wedge (({\sim}Q)\vee  P) = (P\to  Q)\wedge (Q\to  P) = P\leftrightarrow  Q$ (equivalent).
(A) ${\sim}P\vee  Q$ = T, F, T, T; (B) = F, F, F, T; (C) ${\sim}Q\vee  P$ = T, T, F, T. None of them equals the column T, F, F, T.
Answer: (D).
questions.source_note: PDF gives the table for r => s and then an (incomplete) verbal check of option (A); the evaluation of D and of the rest was completed.

alternate_solutions.idea: Simplify $r$ algebraically: ${\sim}P\wedge  Q$ is already inside ${\sim}(P\wedge  Q)$, so $r={\sim}(P\wedge  Q)$.
solution: ${\sim}P \wedge  Q$ implies ${\sim}P$, which implies ${\sim}(P\wedge  Q)$; so $r = {\sim}(P\wedge  Q)\vee ({\sim}P\wedge  Q) = {\sim}(P\wedge  Q) = {\sim}P\vee {\sim}Q$.
The statement is $({\sim}P\vee {\sim}Q)\to ({\sim}P\wedge {\sim}Q)$ $= (P\wedge  Q)\vee ({\sim}P\wedge {\sim}Q)$.
$(P\wedge  Q)\vee ({\sim}P\wedge {\sim}Q) = P\leftrightarrow  Q$ ('both true or both false'), and option (D) is $(P\to  Q)\wedge (Q\to  P)=P\leftrightarrow  Q$. Answer: (D).

useful_results: $P \leftrightarrow  Q \equiv  (P \wedge  Q) \vee  ({\sim}P \wedge  {\sim}Q) \equiv  (P \to  Q) \wedge  (Q \to  P) \equiv  ({\sim}P \vee  Q) \wedge  ({\sim}Q \vee  P)$.
$X \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y) \equiv  X \vee  Y$: here ${\sim}(P\wedge  Q) \vee  ({\sim}P \wedge  Q)$ is ${\sim}P \vee  {\sim}Q$.
${\sim}(P \wedge  Q) \to  ({\sim}P \wedge  {\sim}Q) \equiv  P \leftrightarrow  Q$: 'if not both, then neither' holds exactly when $P$ and $Q$ agree.

questions.question: Let $p$ and $q$ be two statements. Then ${\sim}(p \wedge  (p \to  {\sim}q))$ is equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: $p\wedge (p\to {\sim}q)$ is just $p\wedge {\sim}q$ (modus ponens), so its negation is ${\sim}p\vee  q$.
solution: ${\sim}(p \wedge  (p \to  {\sim}q)) = {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}(p \to  {\sim}q)$.
$p \to  {\sim}q \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q$, so ${\sim}(p \to  {\sim}q) = p \wedge  q$.
Hence the expression is ${\sim}p \vee  (p \wedge  q)$.
Distribute: $({\sim}p \vee  p) \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  q) = \mathrm{t} \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  q)$.
$= {\sim}p \vee  q$. Answer: (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Simplify the inside first: given $p$, the conditional $p\to {\sim}q$ is just ${\sim}q$.
solution: $p \wedge  (p \to  {\sim}q) \equiv  p \wedge  {\sim}q$ (a true $p$ turns $p\to {\sim}q$ into ${\sim}q$).
Negation: ${\sim}(p\wedge {\sim}q) = {\sim}p \vee  q$.
Check (A): $p\vee (p\wedge {\sim}q)=p$; (B): $p\vee (p\wedge  q)=p$; (C): $p\vee ({\sim}p\wedge  q)=p\vee  q$. None equals ${\sim}p\vee  q$. Answer: (D).

useful_results: $X \wedge  (X \to  Y) \equiv  X \wedge  Y$ (modus-ponens simplification).
$X \vee  (X \wedge  Y) \equiv  X$ (absorption) and $X \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y) \equiv  X \vee  Y$.
${\sim}(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \equiv  p \to  q$.

questions.question: The statement $(p \wedge  ({\sim}q)) \to  (p \to  ({\sim}q))$ is:
questions.key_idea: If $p\wedge {\sim}q$ holds then ${\sim}q$ holds, so $p\to {\sim}q$ holds.
solution: Case I, $q=T$: $p\wedge {\sim}q$ is false, so the conditional is true (false premise).
Case II, $q=F$: $p\to {\sim}q=p\to  T=T$, so the conditional is true (true conclusion).
In both cases the statement is true: it is a tautology.
Answer: (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Algebra: remove the conditionals.
solution: $(p\wedge {\sim}q)\to (p\to {\sim}q) = {\sim}(p\wedge {\sim}q) \vee  ({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q)$.
$= ({\sim}p \vee  q) \vee  ({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q) = {\sim}p \vee  (q \vee  {\sim}q) = {\sim}p \vee  \mathrm{t} = \mathrm{t}$.
A tautology, so (A). Answer: (A).

useful_results: $(p \wedge  X) \to  (p \to  X)$ is a tautology for every statement $X$ (here $X={\sim}q$).
A statement that is true whether $q$ is true or false (case split) is a tautology.
A tautology is not equivalent to $p\vee  q$ or to ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}q$, which are false in some row.

questions.question: Let $\Delta,\nabla \in \{\wedge ,\ \vee \}$ be such that $(p \to  q)\,\Delta\,(p\,\nabla\, q)$ is a tautology. Then:
questions.key_idea: $p\to  q$ is false only at $(T,F)$; the second part must be true there and $\Delta$ must be $\vee$.
solution: Rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF: $p\to  q$ = T, F, T, T.
$\Delta=\wedge ,\ \nabla=\vee$: $p\vee  q$ = T, T, T, F; conjunction = T, F, T, F. Not a tautology.
$\Delta=\vee ,\ \nabla=\wedge$: $p\wedge  q$ = T, F, F, F; disjunction = T, F, T, T. Not a tautology.
$\Delta=\vee ,\ \nabla=\vee$: $(p\to  q)\vee (p\vee  q)$ = T, T, T, T. A tautology.
$\Delta=\wedge ,\ \nabla=\wedge$: $(p\to  q)\wedge (p\wedge  q)$ = T, F, F, F. Not a tautology.
Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: The only row where $p\to  q$ fails is $(T,F)$; track it.
solution: $\Delta=\wedge$: the conjunction is false wherever $p\to  q$ is false, i.e. at $(T,F)$. Not a tautology (rules out (A), (B)).
$\Delta=\vee$: the disjunction can fail only at $(T,F)$, so we need $p\nabla q$ true at $(T,F)$.
At $(T,F)$: $p\vee  q = T$ but $p\wedge  q = F$. So $\nabla=\vee$.
Answer: (C).

useful_results: A conjunction with a non-tautology is never a tautology; a disjunction repairs the one failing row.
$(p \to  q) \vee  (p \vee  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  q \vee  p \vee  q \equiv  \mathrm{t}$.
$p\to  q$ is false only at $(T,F)$, where $p\vee  q$ is true.

questions.question: If $p,\ q$ and $r$ are three propositions, then which of the following combinations of truth values of $p,\ q$ and $r$ makes the logical expression $\{(p \vee  q) \wedge  (({\sim}p) \vee  r)\} \to  (({\sim}q) \vee  r)$ false?
questions.key_idea: A false conditional needs $({\sim}q)\vee  r$ false, i.e. $q=T,\ r=F$, and then the premise reduces to ${\sim}p$.
solution: The conditional is false only if the premise is true and $({\sim}q)\vee  r$ is false.
$({\sim}q)\vee  r$ false means ${\sim}q=F$ and $r=F$: $q=T,\ r=F$.
Premise with $q=T,\ r=F$: $(p\vee  T)\wedge ({\sim}p\vee  F) = T \wedge  {\sim}p = {\sim}p$.
For the premise to be true, $p=F$.
So the only false row is $(p,q,r)=(F,T,F)$: option (A).
Check the others: (B) $(T,F,T)$ has ${\sim}q\vee  r=T$; (C) $(T,T,F)$ has premise $T\wedge (F\vee  F)=F$; (D) $(T,F,F)$ has ${\sim}q=T$. Each gives a true conditional.
Answer: (A).
questions.correction_note: PDF's closing line 'Option (3) (p v q) ^ (~q v r) -> (~p v r) will be False' prints a different expression from the question (the premise and conclusion are transposed). The truth-table columns it prints, (p v q) ^ (~p v r) and ~q v r, are correct and give option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute the four options.
solution: (A) $(F,T,F)$: $p\vee  q=T$, ${\sim}p\vee  r=T$, premise $T$; ${\sim}q\vee  r = F\vee  F=F$. Conditional $T\to  F=F$.
(B) $(T,F,T)$: conclusion ${\sim}q\vee  r=T$, so the conditional is true.
(C) $(T,T,F)$: ${\sim}p\vee  r=F\vee  F=F$, premise false, conditional true.
(D) $(T,F,F)$: conclusion ${\sim}q\vee  r=T$, conditional true. Answer: (A).

useful_results: A conditional is false iff premise true and conclusion false; start from the conclusion when it is a short disjunction (false in exactly one way).
$(p \vee  q) \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  r) \to  (q \vee  r)$ is the resolution rule, a tautology; here the conclusion is ${\sim}q\vee  r$, which is not.
Always set up a table with the sub-statements as columns.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
questions.question: The statement $B \to  (({\sim}A) \vee  B)$ is equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: $B\to (\cdot\vee  B)$ is a tautology; so the equivalent options are exactly the tautologous ones.
solution: $B \to  ({\sim}A \vee  B) \equiv  {\sim}B \vee  ({\sim}A \vee  B) = ({\sim}B \vee  B) \vee  {\sim}A = \mathrm{t}$: the given statement is a tautology.
So an option is equivalent to it iff it is also a tautology.
(A): $B \to  (A \to  B) = {\sim}B \vee  ({\sim}A \vee  B) = \mathrm{t}$. Tautology, equivalent.
(B): $A \to  (A \leftrightarrow  B)$; when $A$ is true $A\leftrightarrow  B$ is $B$, so this is $A \to  B = {\sim}A \vee  B$, false at $A=T,\ B=F$. Not a tautology, not equivalent.
(C): $B \to  ({\sim}A \to  B) = {\sim}B \vee  (A \vee  B) = \mathrm{t}$. Tautology, equivalent.
(D): $A \to  ({\sim}A \to  B) = {\sim}A \vee  (A \vee  B) = \mathrm{t}$. Tautology, equivalent.
Correct options: (A), (C), (D).
questions.source_note: PDF shows (A) and says 'similarly' for (C), (D); the rejection of (B) and the three verifications are written out. Official NTA answer (1, 3, 4) agrees.

alternate_solutions.idea: Argue with the premise of each implication instead of algebra.
solution: Each option is an implication $X \to  Y$; it can only fail if $X$ is true and $Y$ false.
(A) $B\to (A\to  B)$: if $B$ is true then $A\to  B$ is true (true conclusion). Never fails.
(C) $B\to ({\sim}A\to  B)$: if $B$ is true then ${\sim}A\to  B$ is true. Never fails.
(D) $A\to ({\sim}A\to  B)$: if $A$ is true then ${\sim}A$ is false so ${\sim}A\to  B$ is true (false premise). Never fails.
(B) $A\to (A\leftrightarrow  B)$: at $A=T,\ B=F$ the conclusion $A\leftrightarrow  B$ is false. Fails. Hence (A), (C), (D).

useful_results: $B \to  (X \vee  B)$, $B \to  (A \to  B)$ and $A \to  ({\sim}A \to  B)$ are all tautologies.
$A \to  (A \leftrightarrow  B) \equiv  A \to  B$: a leading $A$ makes the inner $A$ true.
Equivalent to a tautology means being a tautology: tabulating the options as tautology or not is enough.

questions.question:
Among the statements:
(S1) $((p \vee  q) \to  r) \leftrightarrow  (p \to  r)$
(S2) $((p \vee  q) \to  r) \leftrightarrow  ((p \to  r) \vee  (q \to  r))$
questions.key_idea: $(p\vee  q)\to  r$ equals $(p\to  r)\wedge (q\to  r)$; a single counter-row $p=F,\ q=T,\ r=F$ breaks both statements.
solution: Take $p=F,\ q=T,\ r=F$.
$p\vee  q = T$, so $(p\vee  q)\to  r = T\to  F = F$.
$p\to  r = F\to  F = T$.
(S1): $F \leftrightarrow  T = F$. So (S1) is not a tautology.
$q\to  r = T\to  F = F$, so $(p\to  r)\vee (q\to  r) = T\vee  F = T$.
(S2): $F \leftrightarrow  T = F$. So (S2) is not a tautology.
Neither is a tautology. Answer: (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the identity $(p\vee  q)\to  r \equiv  (p\to  r)\wedge (q\to  r)$ and compare with the claimed forms.
solution: $(p\vee  q)\to  r = {\sim}(p\vee  q)\vee  r = ({\sim}p\wedge {\sim}q)\vee  r = ({\sim}p\vee  r)\wedge ({\sim}q\vee  r) = (p\to  r)\wedge (q\to  r)$.
(S1) claims this equals just $p\to  r$: false when $p\to  r$ is true but $q\to  r$ is false.
(S2) claims the AND equals the OR $(p\to  r)\vee (q\to  r)$: false when exactly one of $p\to  r$, $q\to  r$ is true.
Both fail, e.g. at $p=F,\ q=T,\ r=F$. Answer: (A).

useful_results: $(p \vee  q) \to  r \equiv  (p \to  r) \wedge  (q \to  r)$, whereas $(p \wedge  q) \to  r \equiv  (p \to  r) \vee  (q \to  r)$.
A conjunction is generally not equivalent to a single conjunct or to the disjunction of the conjuncts.
One counter-row suffices to show a statement is not a tautology.

concepts: Translation of statements into symbolic form
questions.question: Consider the following statements: $P$: I have fever. $Q$: I will not take medicine. $R$: I will take rest. The statement 'If I have fever, then I will take medicine and I will take rest' is equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: 'Take medicine' is ${\sim}Q$ (since $Q$ says 'will not take'), so the statement is $P\to ({\sim}Q\wedge  R)$.
solution: 'I will take medicine' is ${\sim}Q$ and 'I will take rest' is $R$.
The statement is $P \to  ({\sim}Q \wedge  R)$.
Remove the conditional: ${\sim}P \vee  ({\sim}Q \wedge  R)$.
Distribute: $({\sim}P \vee  {\sim}Q) \wedge  ({\sim}P \vee  R)$.
This is option (C). Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate options with two test assignments.
solution: Take $(P,Q,R)=(T,T,T)$: he does not take medicine ($Q=T$), so the statement is $T\to  F=F$.
At this row (A) $=(F\vee  T)\wedge (F\vee  F)=F$, (B) $=(T\vee  F)\wedge (T\vee  F)=T$, (C) $=(F\vee  F)\wedge (F\vee  T)=F$, (D) $=(T\vee  T)\wedge (F\vee  T)=T$. So (B), (D) are rejected.
Take $(P,Q,R)=(T,F,T)$: he takes medicine and rest, so the statement is $T\to  T=T$.
At this row (A) $=(F\vee  F)\wedge (F\vee  F)=F$ (wrong) and (C) $=(F\vee  T)\wedge (F\vee  T)=T$ (right). So (A) is rejected.
Hence (C). Answer: (C).

useful_results: $X \to  (Y \wedge  Z) \equiv  (X \to  Y) \wedge  (X \to  Z) \equiv  ({\sim}X \vee  Y) \wedge  ({\sim}X \vee  Z)$.
When $Q$ is a negative statement ('will not'), its negation ${\sim}Q$ is the positive action: translate carefully.
The statement is true whenever $P$ is false, whatever $Q$ and $R$ are.

questions.question:
(S1) $(p \to  q) \vee  (p \wedge  ({\sim}q))$ is a tautology
(S2) $(({\sim}p) \to  ({\sim}q)) \wedge  (({\sim}p) \vee  q)$ is a contradiction. Then:
questions.key_idea: $p\wedge {\sim}q$ is exactly ${\sim}(p\to  q)$, so (S1) is $X\vee {\sim}X$; (S2) is $p\leftrightarrow  q$, true when $p=q$, hence not a contradiction.
solution: Rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF.
(S1): $p\to  q$ = T, F, T, T and $p\wedge {\sim}q$ = F, T, F, F, so $(p\to  q)\vee (p\wedge {\sim}q)$ = T, T, T, T: a tautology. (S1) is correct.
(S2): ${\sim}p\to {\sim}q$ = T, T, F, T and ${\sim}p\vee  q$ = T, F, T, T.
$(({\sim}p)\to ({\sim}q))\wedge (({\sim}p)\vee  q)$ = T, F, F, T.
It is true at $p=q=T$ and $p=q=F$ (it equals $p\leftrightarrow  q$), so it is not a contradiction. (S2) is wrong.
Only (S1) is correct. Answer: (C).
questions.correction_note: ANSWER KEY WRONG: the PDF gives (A) 'both correct', but its own second table has T in the rows (T,T) and (F,F) for ((~p)=>(~q)) ^ ((~p) v q), so S2 is not a contradiction (it equals p<->q). Correct answer: (C) only (S1) is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Reduce both statements to something recognisable.
solution: $p\wedge {\sim}q \equiv  {\sim}(p\to  q)$, so (S1) is $X\vee {\sim}X$ with $X=p\to  q$: a tautology.
${\sim}p\to {\sim}q \equiv  q\to  p$ and ${\sim}p\vee  q \equiv  p\to  q$, so (S2) is $(q\to  p)\wedge (p\to  q) = p\leftrightarrow  q$.
$p\leftrightarrow  q$ is true at $p=q=T$, so (S2) is not a contradiction. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $X \vee  {\sim}X$ is a tautology; $X \wedge  {\sim}X$ is a contradiction; $(p\to  q) \wedge  (q\to  p) \equiv  p \leftrightarrow  q$ is neither.
${\sim}p \to  {\sim}q \equiv  q \to  p$ (contrapositive).
Never trust a key without checking: here the printed table contradicts the printed answer.

questions.question: The number of values of $r \in \{p, q, {\sim}p, {\sim}q\}$ for which $((p \wedge  q) \to  (r \vee  q)) \wedge  ((p \wedge  r) \to  q)$ is a tautology, is:
questions.key_idea: $(p\wedge  q)\to (r\vee  q)$ is always true (the conclusion contains $q$), so only $(p\wedge  r)\to  q$ matters, and it fails only at $p=T,\ q=F,\ r=T$.
solution: $(p\wedge  q)\to (r\vee  q) \equiv  {\sim}(p\wedge  q) \vee  r \vee  q = {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q \vee  q \vee  r = \mathrm{t}$.
So the whole statement is a tautology iff $(p\wedge  r)\to  q$ is.
$(p\wedge  r)\to  q$ is false only if $p=T,\ r=T,\ q=F$.
$r=p$: at $p=T,\ q=F$, $r=T$, so it fails. $r={\sim}q$: at $p=T,\ q=F$, $r=T$, so it fails.
$r=q$: $(p\wedge  q)\to  q$ is a tautology. $r={\sim}p$: $(p\wedge {\sim}p)\to  q=\mathrm{c}\to  q = \mathrm{t}$, a tautology.
So exactly two values, $r=q$ and $r={\sim}p$, work.
Answer: (B) 2.
questions.correction_note: PDF's first line is written as 'p v q -> (r v q) ^ ((p ^ r) -> q)', i.e. with a v and wrong bracketing (the conjunction is made part of the conclusion). Read correctly the statement is [(p^q)->(r v q)] ^ [(p^r)->q]; the PDF's later lines reach the same conclusion. It names only r = ~p and r = q, and does not examine r = p and r = ~q, which are added here.

alternate_solutions.idea: Only the single row $(p,q)=(T,F)$ can cause trouble: require $r$ to be false there.
solution: $(p\wedge  r)\to  q$ fails only when $p=T,\ q=F$ and $r=T$.
So $r$ must be F in the row $(p,q)=(T,F)$ (the rows with $p=F$ or $q=T$ are automatically safe).
Evaluate each candidate at $(T,F)$: $r=p\to T$; $r=q\to F$; $r={\sim}p\to F$; $r={\sim}q\to T$.
Exactly two candidates ($q$ and ${\sim}p$) give F. Answer: (B) 2.

useful_results: $(p \wedge  q) \to  (r \vee  q)$ is a tautology for every $r$, because its conclusion already contains $q$.
$(p \wedge  r) \to  q$ fails in exactly one row: $p=T,\ r=T,\ q=F$; to repair it choose $r$ false in the row $(p,q)=(T,F)$.
For counting questions on a statement with an unknown $r$, reduce the check to the failing rows.

concepts: Negation and simplification of compound statements
questions.question: The negation of the expression $q \vee  (({\sim}q) \wedge  p)$ is equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: $q\vee ({\sim}q\wedge  p)$ simplifies to $q\vee  p$, so its negation is ${\sim}p\wedge {\sim}q$.
solution: ${\sim}(q \vee  (({\sim}q) \wedge  p)) = {\sim}q \wedge  {\sim}(({\sim}q) \wedge  p)$.
${\sim}(({\sim}q) \wedge  p) = q \vee  {\sim}p$, so this is ${\sim}q \wedge  (q \vee  {\sim}p)$.
Distribute: $({\sim}q \wedge  q) \vee  ({\sim}q \wedge  {\sim}p)$.
${\sim}q \wedge  q \equiv  \mathrm{c}$, so the result is $\mathrm{c} \vee  ({\sim}q \wedge  {\sim}p) = {\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q$.
Answer: (B).
questions.source_note: Option (D) is printed with a stray symbol (a multiplication sign); it is not a valid statement and is irrelevant to the answer.

alternate_solutions.idea: Simplify before negating: the term ${\sim}q\wedge  p$ only helps $q\vee \cdot$ when $q$ is false.
solution: $q \vee  ({\sim}q \wedge  p) \equiv  (q \vee  {\sim}q) \wedge  (q \vee  p) \equiv  q \vee  p$.
Negation: ${\sim}(q\vee  p) = {\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q$. Answer: (B).

useful_results: $X \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y) \equiv  X \vee  Y$ (absorption of the negated term).
${\sim}(X \vee  Y) \equiv  {\sim}X \wedge  {\sim}Y$.
A disjunction is false only when every disjunct is false: here $q=F$ and $p=F$.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is a tautology?
questions.key_idea: $({\sim}p)\to  q$ is $p\vee  q$, which is implied by $p\wedge  q$.
solution: (A): $p \to  (p \wedge  (p \to  q)) = {\sim}p \vee  (p \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  q)) = {\sim}p \vee  ((p \wedge  {\sim}p) \vee  (p \wedge  q)) = {\sim}p \vee  (p \wedge  q)$.
${\sim}p \vee  (p \wedge  q) = ({\sim}p \vee  p) \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  q) = {\sim}p \vee  q$, which is false at $p=T,\ q=F$. Not a tautology.
(B): $p \vee  (p \wedge  q) = p$ (absorption), false at $p=F$. Not a tautology.
(C): $(p \wedge  q) \to  ({\sim}p \to  q) = {\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  (p \vee  q) = ({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q) \vee  (p \vee  q) = \mathrm{t}$. A tautology.
(D): $(p \wedge  (p \to  q)) \to  {\sim}q = {\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  {\sim}q = {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q$, false at $p=q=T$. Not a tautology.
Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Falsifier search for (C): the premise $p\wedge  q$ forces everything true.
solution: (C) fails only if $p\wedge  q$ is true and ${\sim}p\to  q$ false.
$p\wedge  q$ true means $p=q=T$; then ${\sim}p\to  q=F\to  T=T$. So (C) never fails.
The other options have easy counter-rows: (A) at $(T,F)$, (B) at $(F,*)$, (D) at $(T,T)$. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $(p \wedge  q) \to  (p \vee  q)$ is a tautology (conjunction implies disjunction); ${\sim}p \to  q \equiv  p \vee  q$.
$p \wedge  (p \to  q) \equiv  p \wedge  q$ and $p \to  (p \wedge  q) \equiv  p \to  q$.
Absorption: $p \vee  (p \wedge  q) \equiv  p$.

questions.question: The statement $(P \to  Q) \wedge  (R \to  Q)$ is logically equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: Two conditionals with the same conclusion combine through the premises' disjunction: $(P\to  Q)\wedge (R\to  Q)\equiv (P\vee  R)\to  Q$.
solution: $P \to  Q \equiv  {\sim}P \vee  Q$, so the statement is $({\sim}P \vee  Q) \wedge  ({\sim}R \vee  Q)$.
Factor out $Q$: $= ({\sim}P \wedge  {\sim}R) \vee  Q$.
De Morgan: ${\sim}P \wedge  {\sim}R = {\sim}(P \vee  R)$.
So the statement is ${\sim}(P \vee  R) \vee  Q = (P \vee  R) \to  Q$.
Answer: (A).
questions.source_note: PDF jumps from (~P v Q) ^ (~R v Q) to ~(P v R) v Q; the factoring step and De Morgan are written out.

alternate_solutions.idea: The statement is false in exactly the rows where $Q$ is false and at least one of $P,R$ is true; compare with each option.
solution: $(P\to  Q)\wedge (R\to  Q)$ is false iff $P\to  Q$ is false or $R\to  Q$ is false, i.e. $Q=F$ and ($P=T$ or $R=T$).
$(P\vee  R)\to  Q$ is false iff $P\vee  R$ true and $Q$ false: the same rows.
(B) is false only if $P=R=T,\ Q=F$ (fewer rows); (C), (D) are about $R$ as conclusion, not $Q$. Answer: (A).

useful_results: $(P \to  Q) \wedge  (R \to  Q) \equiv  (P \vee  R) \to  Q$ and $(P \to  Q) \vee  (R \to  Q) \equiv  (P \wedge  R) \to  Q$.
$(P \to  Q) \wedge  (P \to  R) \equiv  P \to  (Q \wedge  R)$ and $(P \to  Q) \vee  (P \to  R) \equiv  P \to  (Q \vee  R)$.
Rule of thumb: a common premise turns into a conjunction/disjunction of conclusions, a common conclusion turns into the opposite connective of premises.

questions.question:
Among the statements
(S1): $(p \to  q) \vee  (({\sim}p) \wedge  q)$ is a tautology
(S2): $(q \to  p) \to  (({\sim}p) \wedge  q)$ is a contradiction
questions.key_idea: (S1) equals ${\sim}p\vee  q$ (false at $(T,F)$); (S2) equals ${\sim}p\wedge  q$ (true at $(F,T)$): neither claim holds.
solution: Rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF.
(S1): $p\to  q$ = T, F, T, T and ${\sim}p\wedge  q$ = F, F, T, F, so $(p\to  q)\vee ({\sim}p\wedge  q)$ = T, F, T, T. The row TF is F, so (S1) is not a tautology.
(S2): $q\to  p$ = T, T, F, T and ${\sim}p\wedge  q$ = F, F, T, F.
$(q\to  p)\to ({\sim}p\wedge  q)$ = F, F, T, F.
The row FT is T, so (S2) is not a contradiction.
Neither claim is true. Answer: (B).
questions.correction_note: PDF's table for (S2) has the header '(p=>q) => (~p ^ q)' where the statement is (q=>p) => (~p ^ q); the printed values F,F,T,F are those of the correct statement.

alternate_solutions.idea: Simplify each statement algebraically.
solution: (S1): $({\sim}p\vee  q)\vee ({\sim}p\wedge  q) = {\sim}p\vee  q$, which is false at $p=T,\ q=F$. Not a tautology.
(S2): $(q\to  p)\to ({\sim}p\wedge  q) = {\sim}(q\to  p)\vee ({\sim}p\wedge  q) = (q\wedge {\sim}p)\vee ({\sim}p\wedge  q) = {\sim}p\wedge  q$.
${\sim}p\wedge  q$ is true at $p=F,\ q=T$: not a contradiction.
Answer: (B).

useful_results: $X \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y) \equiv  X \vee  Y$ and ${\sim}(q \to  p) \equiv  q \wedge  {\sim}p$.
Check by simplification: $(q \to  p) \to  ({\sim}p \wedge  q) \equiv  {\sim}p \wedge  q$.
A statement is a tautology iff it is true in every row and a contradiction iff it is false in every row; a single row refutes each claim.

questions.question: Negation of $(p \to  q) \to  (q \to  p)$ is:
questions.key_idea: ${\sim}(X\to  Y) = X\wedge {\sim}Y$: the negation is $(p\to  q)\wedge (q\wedge {\sim}p)$, and $q\wedge {\sim}p$ already makes $p\to  q$ true.
solution: $(p \to  q) \to  (q \to  p) \equiv  {\sim}(p \to  q) \vee  (q \to  p) = (p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  ({\sim}q \vee  p)$.
$p \wedge  {\sim}q$ is contained in ${\sim}q \vee  p$, so the expression is $p \vee  {\sim}q$.
Negation: ${\sim}(p \vee  {\sim}q) = {\sim}p \wedge  q$.
So the negation is $q \wedge  {\sim}p$. Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the only row where the conditional fails.
solution: $(p\to  q)\to (q\to  p)$ is false iff $p\to  q$ is true and $q\to  p$ is false.
$q\to  p$ false means $q=T,\ p=F$; then $p\to  q = F\to  T = T$ as required.
So the negation is true only at $p=F,\ q=T$, which is $q\wedge {\sim}p$. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $(p \to  q) \to  (q \to  p) \equiv  q \to  p \equiv  p \vee  {\sim}q$ (it is false only at $(F,T)$).
${\sim}(X \to  Y) \equiv  X \wedge  {\sim}Y$ turns a 'conditional negation' into a one-row condition.
In general $(X \to  Y) \to  (Y \to  X) \equiv  Y \to  X$: the extra conditional $X\to  Y$ in the premise adds no information.

questions.question: The negation of $(p \wedge  ({\sim}q)) \vee  ({\sim}p)$ is equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: $(p\wedge {\sim}q)\vee {\sim}p$ simplifies to ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}q$, so its negation is $p\wedge  q$.
solution: ${\sim}[(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  {\sim}p] = {\sim}(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \wedge  p$.
${\sim}(p \wedge  {\sim}q) = {\sim}p \vee  q$, so this is $({\sim}p \vee  q) \wedge  p$.
Distribute: $({\sim}p \wedge  p) \vee  (q \wedge  p) = \mathrm{c} \vee  (q \wedge  p)$.
$= p \wedge  q$. Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: A disjunction is false only if both disjuncts are false.
solution: $(p\wedge {\sim}q)\vee {\sim}p$ is false iff ${\sim}p$ is false ($p=T$) and $p\wedge {\sim}q$ is false (so $q=T$).
So the negation is true exactly at $p=q=T$: $p\wedge  q$. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  {\sim}p \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q \equiv  {\sim}(p \wedge  q)$.
$X \vee  ({\sim}X \wedge  Y)$-pattern: here ${\sim}p \vee  (p \wedge  {\sim}q) = {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q$.
A disjunction of literals/terms is false in the rows where every disjunct is false.

questions.question: The negation of the statement $(p \vee  q) \wedge  (q \vee  ({\sim}r))$ is:
questions.key_idea: De Morgan gives $({\sim}p\wedge {\sim}q)\vee ({\sim}q\wedge  r)$, and ${\sim}q$ is a common factor.
solution: ${\sim}((p \vee  q) \wedge  (q \vee  {\sim}r)) = {\sim}(p \vee  q) \vee  {\sim}(q \vee  {\sim}r)$.
$= ({\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  ({\sim}q \wedge  r)$.
Factor ${\sim}q$: $= {\sim}q \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  r)$.
$= ({\sim}p \vee  r) \wedge  {\sim}q$. Answer: (C).
questions.source_note: PDF reaches the same result by distributing and factoring $({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q)$ in a longer way; shortened here by factoring the common ${\sim}q$ (same logic).

alternate_solutions.idea: Test assignments to eliminate the three wrong options.
solution: Row $(T,F,T)$: the statement is $T\wedge (F\vee  F)=F$, so the negation is True. (A) $=(F\vee  T)\wedge  F=F$: rejected.
Row $(T,T,F)$: the statement is $T\wedge (T\vee  T)=T$, so the negation is False. (B) $=(F\vee  F)\vee  T=T$: rejected.
Row $(F,F,F)$: the statement is $(F\vee  F)\wedge (\dots)=F$, so the negation is True. (D) $=(F\vee  F)\wedge  T=F$: rejected.
(C) agrees on all three rows. Answer: (C).

useful_results: ${\sim}[(X \vee  Y) \wedge  (Y \vee  Z)] \equiv  ({\sim}X \wedge  {\sim}Y) \vee  ({\sim}Y \wedge  {\sim}Z) \equiv  {\sim}Y \wedge  ({\sim}X \vee  {\sim}Z)$.
Factoring a common literal out of a disjunction of conjunctions saves a long distribution.
Three well-chosen rows can eliminate three options.

concepts: Negation and simplification of compound statements
questions.question: The statement ${\sim}[p \vee  ({\sim}(p \wedge  q))]$ is equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: $p\vee {\sim}(p\wedge  q)$ is a tautology, so its negation is a contradiction; only (A) is a contradiction.
solution: ${\sim}[p \vee  {\sim}(p \wedge  q)] = {\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}{\sim}(p \wedge  q)$.
${\sim}{\sim}(p \wedge  q) = p \wedge  q$, so this is ${\sim}p \wedge  (p \wedge  q)$.
$= (p \wedge  q) \wedge  {\sim}p$, option (A) (a contradiction since it contains $p$ and ${\sim}p$).
The other options are not contradictions: (B) ${\sim}p\wedge {\sim}q$ is true at $p=q=F$; (C) ${\sim}p\vee {\sim}q$ is true at $p=F$; (D) ${\sim}p\wedge  q$ is true at $(F,T)$.
Answer: (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Show that the inside is a tautology.
solution: $p \vee  {\sim}(p \wedge  q) = p \vee  {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q = \mathrm{t}$.
The negation of a tautology is a contradiction.
Option (A) $(p\wedge  q)\wedge {\sim}p$ contains $p$ and ${\sim}p$ in a conjunction: a contradiction. The others are true in some row. Answer: (A).

useful_results: $p \vee  {\sim}(p \wedge  q) \equiv  \mathrm{t}$ (if $p$ is false, $p\wedge  q$ is false).
The negation of a tautology is a contradiction (fallacy), and vice versa.
Two contradictions are equivalent to each other.

questions.question: The converse of $(({\sim}p) \wedge  q) \to  r$ is:
questions.key_idea: The converse of $X\to  r$ is $r\to  X$ with $X={\sim}p\wedge  q$; by contraposition it equals ${\sim}X\to {\sim}r = (p\vee {\sim}q)\to {\sim}r$.
solution: The converse of $X \to  r$ is $r \to  X$, here $r \to  (({\sim}p) \wedge  q)$.
Take its contrapositive: $r \to  X \equiv  {\sim}X \to  {\sim}r$.
${\sim}X = {\sim}({\sim}p \wedge  q) = p \vee  {\sim}q$.
So the converse is logically equivalent to $(p \vee  {\sim}q) \to  {\sim}r$, which is option (A).

Check the rest: (B) ${\sim}r\to (p\wedge  q) = r\vee (p\wedge  q)$, (C) ${\sim}r\to ({\sim}p\wedge  q) = r\vee ({\sim}p\wedge  q)$ and (D) $({\sim}p\vee  q)\to  r$ are not equivalent to ${\sim}r\vee ({\sim}p\wedge  q)$.
Answer: (A).
questions.correction_note: PDF writes converse = r => (~p ^ q) = ~r v (~p ^ q) and then '= ~r v (p v ~q) = (p v ~q) => ~r'. The step ~r v (~p ^ q) -> ~r v (p v ~q) is wrong (it negates the bracket without the matching negation of the implication); the correct step is the contraposition r => X = ~X => ~r with ~X = p v ~q. The final option (A) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compare the falsifying rows of the converse and of option (A).
solution: $r\to ({\sim}p\wedge  q)$ is false iff $r=T$ and ${\sim}p\wedge  q$ is false, i.e. $r=T$ and ($p=T$ or $q=F$).
(A) $(p\vee {\sim}q)\to {\sim}r$ is false iff $p\vee {\sim}q$ is true and ${\sim}r$ false, i.e. $r=T$ and ($p=T$ or $q=F$). Same rows.
Answer: (A).

useful_results: For $X \to  Y$: converse $Y \to  X$, inverse ${\sim}X \to  {\sim}Y$, contrapositive ${\sim}Y \to  {\sim}X$. Converse and inverse are equivalent; the contrapositive equals the original.
The 'converse' written in contrapositive form is the standard way JEE options disguise it.
$Y \to  X \equiv  {\sim}X \to  {\sim}Y$.

questions.question:
Among the two statements
(S1): $(p \to  q) \wedge  (p \wedge  ({\sim}q))$ is a contradiction and
(S2): $(p \wedge  q) \vee  (({\sim}p) \wedge  q) \vee  (p \wedge  ({\sim}q)) \vee  (({\sim}p) \wedge  ({\sim}q))$ is a tautology:
questions.key_idea: (S1) is ${\sim}X\wedge  X$ for $X=p\to  q$; (S2) lists all four rows $(p,q)$, so exactly one disjunct is true each time.
solution: (S1): rows $(p,q)=$ TT, TF, FT, FF: $p\to  q$ = T, F, T, T and $p\wedge {\sim}q$ = F, T, F, F.
$(p\to  q)\wedge (p\wedge {\sim}q)$ = F, F, F, F. Always false: (S1) is a contradiction.
(S2): the four disjuncts are $p\wedge  q$, ${\sim}p\wedge  q$, $p\wedge {\sim}q$, ${\sim}p\wedge {\sim}q$.
Their truth values by row are TT: T,F,F,F; TF: F,F,T,F; FT: F,T,F,F; FF: F,F,F,T.
Each row makes exactly one disjunct true, so (S2) is true in every row: a tautology.
Both statements are true. Answer: (B).
questions.correction_note: PDF's table for S2 labels the second and third columns both as (p ^ ~q); the second must be (~p ^ q) (its values F,F,T,F are those of ~p ^ q). Result unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Logical reasoning without a table.
solution: (S1): $p\wedge {\sim}q$ is exactly ${\sim}(p\to  q)$, so (S1) is $X \wedge  {\sim}X$ for $X=p\to  q$: a contradiction.
(S2): for any $(p,q)$ exactly one of the four conjunctions describes the actual truth values of $p$ and $q$, so the disjunction is always true: a tautology.
Answer: (B).

useful_results: The four 'minterms' $p\wedge  q,\ {\sim}p\wedge  q,\ p\wedge {\sim}q,\ {\sim}p\wedge {\sim}q$ partition all rows, so their disjunction is a tautology; any proper subset of them is not.
$(p \to  q) \wedge  (p \wedge  {\sim}q) \equiv  \mathrm{c}$.
A disjunction of 3 of the 4 minterms is equivalent to the negation of the missing one.

concepts: Negation and simplification of compound statements
questions.question: The negation of the statement $((A \wedge  (B \vee  C)) \to  (A \vee  B)) \to  A$ is:
questions.key_idea: $A\wedge (B\vee  C)\to (A\vee  B)$ is always true, so the statement is $\mathrm{t}\to  A=A$ and its negation is ${\sim}A$.
solution: Let $X=A\wedge (B\vee  C)$ and $Y=A\vee  B$; the statement is $(X\to  Y)\to  A$.
$(X\to  Y)\to  A \equiv  {\sim}({\sim}X\vee  Y)\vee  A = (X \wedge  {\sim}Y) \vee  A$.
$X \wedge  {\sim}Y = A \wedge  (B \vee  C) \wedge  {\sim}A \wedge  {\sim}B = \mathrm{c}$ (it contains $A$ and ${\sim}A$).
So the statement is $\mathrm{c} \vee  A = A$.
The negation is ${\sim}A$. Answer: (C).
questions.source_note: PDF's first line writes the statement without the bracket structure; it is read as (X => Y) => A.

alternate_solutions.idea: Semantic argument: $X\to  Y$ is a tautology.
solution: $A\wedge (B\vee  C)$ true forces $A$ true, which forces $A\vee  B$ true. So $X\to  Y$ is always true.
Then $(X\to  Y)\to  A$ is '$T\to  A$', which has the truth value of $A$.
Its negation has the truth value of ${\sim}A$. Answer: (C).

useful_results: If $X \to  Y$ is a tautology then $(X \to  Y) \to  Z \equiv  Z$.
$A \wedge  (\dots) \to  (A \vee  \dots)$ is always true: a conjunction containing $A$ implies a disjunction containing $A$.
${\sim}((X \to  Y) \to  A) \equiv  (X \to  Y) \wedge  {\sim}A$.

questions.question: The statement $(p \wedge  ({\sim}q)) \vee  (({\sim}p) \wedge  q) \vee  (({\sim}p) \wedge  ({\sim}q))$ is equivalent to:
questions.key_idea: Combine $({\sim}p\wedge  q)\vee ({\sim}p\wedge {\sim}q)={\sim}p$; then ${\sim}p\vee (p\wedge {\sim}q)={\sim}p\vee {\sim}q$.
solution: Group the last two terms: $({\sim}p \wedge  q) \vee  ({\sim}p \wedge  {\sim}q) = {\sim}p \wedge  (q \vee  {\sim}q) = {\sim}p$.
The statement becomes $(p \wedge  {\sim}q) \vee  {\sim}p$.
Distribute: $(p \vee  {\sim}p) \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  {\sim}p) = \mathrm{t} \wedge  ({\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q)$.
$= {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q$. Answer: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Complement: the expression is the disjunction of three of the four rows, so it is the negation of the missing one.
solution: The four possible rows of $(p,q)$ correspond to $p\wedge  q$, $p\wedge {\sim}q$, ${\sim}p\wedge  q$, ${\sim}p\wedge {\sim}q$ and exactly one is true.
The given expression contains the last three, so it is false exactly when $p\wedge  q$ is true.
So it equals ${\sim}(p\wedge  q) = {\sim}p\vee {\sim}q$. Answer: (C).

useful_results: $(X \wedge  Y) \vee  (X \wedge  {\sim}Y) \equiv  X$ (splitting).
A disjunction of $k$ of the $2^n$ minterms is the negation of the disjunction of the remaining ones.
${\sim}p \vee  (p \wedge  {\sim}q) \equiv  {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q$ (absorption of the negated term).

concepts: Negation and simplification of compound statements
questions.question: Negation of $p \wedge  (q \wedge  {\sim}(p \wedge  q))$ is:
questions.key_idea: $q\wedge {\sim}(p\wedge  q)$ is false whenever $q$ is true and $p\wedge  q$ false, i.e. never with the extra $p$: the inside is a contradiction, the negation a tautology.
solution: ${\sim}[p \wedge  (q \wedge  {\sim}(p \wedge  q))] = {\sim}p \vee  ({\sim}q \vee  (p \wedge  q))$.
${\sim}q \vee  (p \wedge  q) = ({\sim}q \vee  p) \wedge  ({\sim}q \vee  q) = ({\sim}q \vee  p) \wedge  \mathrm{t} = {\sim}q \vee  p$.
So the negation is ${\sim}p \vee  ({\sim}q \vee  p) = {\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q \vee  p$.
${\sim}p \vee  {\sim}q \vee  p = {\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  p$, option (A).
It equals $({\sim}p \vee  p) \vee  {\sim}q = \mathrm{t}$.
Answer: (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Show the inside is a contradiction.
solution: $q \wedge  {\sim}(p \wedge  q)$ is true iff $q=T$ and $p\wedge  q$ false, i.e. $q=T,\ p=F$.
Then the extra factor $p$ makes $p \wedge  (\dots)$ false: it is false in every row, a contradiction.
Its negation is a tautology; (A) ${\sim}(p\wedge  q)\vee  p = {\sim}p\vee {\sim}q\vee  p$ is a tautology. (B), (C), (D) are not tautologies. Answer: (A).

useful_results: $X \wedge  {\sim}X \equiv  \mathrm{c}$ with $X=p\wedge  q$ or its parts: a conjunction with a hidden $p\wedge  q$ and ${\sim}(p\wedge  q)$ is a contradiction.
The negation of a contradiction is a tautology, so the answer must be the tautologous option.
${\sim}(p \wedge  q) \vee  p \equiv  \mathrm{t}$.

questions.question: The number of ordered triplets of the truth values of $p,\ q$ and $r$ such that the truth value of the statement $(p \vee  q) \wedge  (p \vee  r) \to  (q \vee  r)$ is true, is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $(p\vee  q)\wedge (p\vee  r)=p\vee (q\wedge  r)$, so the statement fails only when $q\vee  r$ is false but $p$ is true.
solution: There are $2^3=8$ ordered triplets $(p,q,r)$.
List all eight: $p\vee  q$ = T, T, T, T, T, T, F, F and $p\vee  r$ = T, T, T, T, T, F, T, F for $(p,q,r)$ = TTT, TTF, TFT, TFF, FTT, FTF, FFT, FFF.
The premise $(p\vee  q)\wedge (p\vee  r)$ = T, T, T, T, T, F, F, F.
The conclusion $q\vee  r$ = T, T, T, F, T, T, T, F.
The conditional is F only where the premise is T and the conclusion F: row TFF.
So it is true in $8-1=7$ triplets.
Answer: 7.
questions.source_note: PDF gives the 8-row table; the rows are described in text here.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count the failing rows directly.
solution: The conditional is false iff $q\vee  r$ is false and the premise is true.
$q\vee  r$ false forces $q=F,\ r=F$.
Then the premise becomes $(p\vee  F)\wedge (p\vee  F)=p$, which is true iff $p=T$.
So there is exactly one failing triplet, $(T,F,F)$, and $8-1=7$ triplets make the statement true. Answer: 7.

useful_results: $(p \vee  q) \wedge  (p \vee  r) \equiv  p \vee  (q \wedge  r)$ (distribution).
The number of rows where $X\to  Y$ is true is $2^n$ minus the number of rows where $X$ is true and $Y$ is false.
A statement is true in $2^n-1$ rows iff it is false in exactly one row.
